Reading the client IP from the first entry of `x-forwarded-for` without validating a trusted-proxy hop count treats an attacker-controlled header as ground truth: an attacker can send a different fabricated value on every request, so each request lands in a fresh rate-limit bucket and the counter never accumulates past 1 — a complete bypass rather than a partial weakening.

The correct fix for header-based client IP is configuring the trusted proxy chain to the actual hop count (for example `app.set('trust proxy', <hopCount>)`), so the framework strips client-injected entries and keeps only the value appended by the trusted load balancer.

Falling back to a per-process in-memory Map and returning true whenever the Redis-backed counter throws is a fail-open design for a security control: it turns a Redis outage into every replica running its own private, unshared counter, silently multiplying the effective rate limit by replica count and going dark exactly when it's needed most.

An abuse control like a login rate limiter must fail closed on a counter-store error — rejecting the request during an outage costs some availability, but a control that silently opens exactly when a distributed brute-force attack is most likely to be running is worse than no control at all.

Setting `user.locked = true` permanently once failed-login count reaches a threshold, with no code path anywhere to clear it, converts the lockout mechanism into a weapon: anyone who knows a victim's email can lock that account on purpose with five wrong passwords, forcing a support ticket to recover.

A safer response to repeated failed logins is exponential backoff per account combined with a CAPTCHA challenge after repeated failures, since this keeps raising the attacker's cost without ever handing an anonymous requester a permanent-lockout button against someone else's account.

Verifying a fix like this needs adversarial tests, not a single manual check from one tester: a request series rotating a forged `x-forwarded-for` value on every call must still return 429 by the expected attempt, a chaos test with the counter store stopped must show the request rejected rather than admitted, and repeated wrong-password attempts must show growing delay or a CAPTCHA challenge rather than a permanent lock.

Prioritizing PR findings by exploitability rather than by code style separates two complete bypasses — the spoofable rate-limit key and the fail-open counter fallback — from a design flaw with user-facing harm — the permanent lockout — with attacker impact, not stylistic preference, deciding what blocks approval.

Commenting out the per-test cleanup hook while both flows share one test file turns Flow 2 into a hidden dependent of Flow 1: it asserts against the exact row Flow 1 just committed, so filtering to run Flow 2 alone, reordering the tests, or running them in parallel all break it immediately.
When an earlier flow in the same suite fails partway through, every flow that runs after it cascades into a false red even though nothing is actually wrong with that later flow's own logic.

A missing connection-pool teardown is a separate defect from the missing per-test cleanup, not a side effect of it — a suite can have full order independence restored and still leave the app/DataSource open at the end.

`app.close()` is what triggers `onModuleDestroy` and releases resources like the TypeORM connection pool; without it the Postgres socket stays open and the test runner cannot exit the process on its own.

Locally an unclosed handle shows up as a Ctrl+C annoyance, but in CI there is no one to kill the process, so the job runner waits for a natural exit and hangs until it burns its own timeout budget — real pipeline time lost on every run.

`expect(res.body).toEqual({...})` performs a strict deep comparison over the entire response body, so any field the server adds later breaks every test using it even when the core behavior under test is still correct.

Copying the actual received value of a nondeterministic field like `createdAt` into the expected object just to make a `toEqual` assertion pass is a sign the assertion is checking the wrong thing — a shape check such as `expect.any(String)` alongside a narrower `toMatchObject` on the fields that matter targets the real behavior instead.

Preserving the original speed win doesn't require deleting the cleanup outright — narrowing the truncate to only the table or rows the suite actually touches keeps most of the time savings while restoring test independence.

In an e2e suite, wall-clock time decomposes into N × boot cost + N × cleanup cost + N × actual request work; when the requests themselves take milliseconds, the fixture lifecycle (app boot, cleanup, re-seed) — not the tests' own logic — is what dominates the runtime.

A full app boot (compiling the Nest DI container and opening the TypeORM connection) produces a running app that is identical for every test in the file, so building it fresh inside `beforeEach` pays that cost N times for no benefit; moving it to `beforeAll` (or an equivalent once-per-file/shared-fixture scope) collapses N× boot cost to 1×, since what a test needs is a running app, not a newly compiled one.

A per-test `TRUNCATE ... CASCADE` that wipes every table — including reference/master data the tests never mutate — forces that reference data to be re-seeded before every single test even though it never changes; narrowing the truncate to only the tables the tests actually write to removes this redundant re-seed cost.

`RESTART IDENTITY` on a truncate keeps auto-increment IDs from leaking across tests even when the truncate scope is narrowed to just the mutated tables, so shrinking cleanup scope does not require giving up ID predictability between tests.

Reference/master data can be seeded once in `beforeAll` right after the app boots, with the single full-table wipe (including that reference data) deferred to `afterAll` right before the app closes — this replaces N re-seeds with one.

Narrowing what gets rebuilt or truncated per test does not change the isolation guarantee: every test still starts from an empty state for the tables it touches — only the mechanism producing that state gets cheaper, not what is promised to the test author.

Skipping the truncate of tables that tests actually mutate in order to save time is a different kind of change from narrowing cleanup scope: it lets mutated rows leak between tests and trades correctness for speed, which is why it must be rejected even under time pressure.

A speed-up claim needs two kinds of proof: running the suite with shuffled order or single-test (`.only`) isolation confirms no test silently depends on state left behind by another, and a recorded before/after wall-clock measurement confirms the suite actually got faster rather than the improvement being assumed.

A UI e2e suite that repeats a full browser login before every test pays that ~3s cost once per test for zero new information, since login success is already proven after the first test — the resulting suite slowdown scales with the number of tests, not with the number of distinct things being verified.

Recording a trace, video, and screenshot on every run regardless of outcome is a separate, unrelated cost from the login overhead: this data exists to aid debugging, but a passing test is never debugged, so paying the recording cost on passing runs buys nothing.

Playwright's `storageState` mechanism amortizes login across a suite: a `globalSetup` script performs the one real login the suite needs in its own browser context and serializes cookies and localStorage to a file; every other test's context then loads that file via `use.storageState`, starting already authenticated in a few hundred milliseconds instead of repeating the ~3s login flow.

The storage state file must be written only after the post-login redirect is confirmed (e.g., after `page.waitForURL` resolves), not the instant the login click resolves — saving state before the redirect lands bakes a half-authenticated or still-on-login-page session into the file, and every test that loads it then fails for a reason unrelated to what it actually tests.

The spec that verifies the login flow itself must still open a fresh browser context with no `storageState` loaded; reusing the shared authenticated state there would mean the login form is never actually exercised again, silently losing coverage on the exact mechanism the rest of the suite now depends on.

Amortizing login into one stored session introduces a new failure mode: the token baked into the storage state carries its own TTL, and if that TTL is shorter than the total suite runtime, tests running late fail with unrelated 401s that look like flakiness — mitigated by using long-lived tokens in the test environment or re-minting the storage state partway through a long run.

Playwright's `trace`, `video`, and `screenshot` options can be scoped to failure conditions instead of left always-on: `trace: 'on-first-retry'` and `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'` still capture everything needed to diagnose a failing test while adding zero recording cost to tests that pass.

The login-overhead fix and the diagnostics-overhead fix are independent because they have different root causes — redundant repeated work versus unconditional instrumentation — and different solutions — state caching versus conditional recording — so treating them as one problem risks fixing only half the slowdown.

A test that passes in isolation but fails when run alongside others—especially when the failing test changes depending on execution order—signals shared mutable state between tests, not an incorrect assertion count.

Building `mockRepo` with `vi.fn()` at `describe`-scope creates it only ONCE, because Vitest runs the `describe` body a single time per file; that same object, along with its recorded-calls array and any `mockResolvedValue` stub, is reused unmodified by every `it` block inside it.

The `beforeEach` hook here only rebuilds the Nest testing module and re-fetches `service` from it — it never touches `mockRepo`, so nothing resets the mock's call history or stubbed return values between tests.

Because a `vi.fn()`'s call history persists until explicitly cleared, `toHaveBeenCalledOnce()` in one test and `not.toHaveBeenCalled()` in another read from the same accumulating counter rather than a fresh one per test.

Execution order only decides which assertion trips first, not whether the bug exists: swapping the two `it` blocks moves the failure to the other test, since whichever runs second inherits the stale call count left behind by the one that ran first.

This is a violation of the Isolated principle from F.I.R.S.T.: every test must start from a known, clean state, and no test's outcome should depend on which other tests ran before it or in what order.

The one-line fix is calling `vi.clearAllMocks()` as the first statement inside `beforeEach`, before the testing module is rebuilt — it resets every mock's call history and configured return values so each test starts from a clean slate.

Rerunning the file with the tests in their original order, then swapped or shuffled, and seeing green in every ordering confirms the fix; the same file is worth sweeping afterward for other leaks of this class, such as a `vi.useFakeTimers()` call left active without a matching `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`.

A test suite that passes reliably in serial execution but fails intermittently only under parallel execution, with the specific failing test changing between runs, is the signature of cross-process interference rather than a broken assertion — a genuine logic bug in the test would fail the same way every time regardless of how many workers run it.

The cheapest way to confirm a suspected parallelism race is to force the suite back to single-process execution (for Vitest's forks pool, restoring `pool: 'forks', poolOptions: { forks: { singleFork: true } }`) before touching any test code; if that alone makes the suite consistently green, the environment's isolation model is the bug, not the test logic.

When every `*.e2e-spec.ts` file reads the identical `DATABASE_URL` from `.env.test`, running those files as concurrent child processes means all of them are silently sharing one physical Postgres database, even though each file's setup and assertions are written as if it owned the table exclusively.

The exact race is a cross-fork write during another fork's read window: fork B's `afterEach` — `TRUNCATE orders RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE` — or fork B's own `createOrder()` inserts can land at the precise wall-clock moment fork A is between creating its two orders and asserting `toHaveLength(2)`, so A observes 0 rows if it got truncated mid-window or 5 rows if B's inserts landed in the same table just before A's list call.
Which specific test fails is determined by nondeterministic OS process scheduling across forks, which is exactly why the failing assertion moves between CI runs instead of staying fixed on one test.

There are two structurally sound fixes with a clear trade-off: force every e2e file through a single process via `singleFork: true`, which is dead simple and correct by construction but makes the whole suite run wall-clock serial; or keep forks parallel and give each one its own database by deriving the database name from `process.env.VITEST_POOL_ID` (e.g. `appdb_test_${VITEST_POOL_ID}`) and provisioning/migrating it once per pool in a `globalSetup`, which preserves parallel speed at the cost of extra per-worker infrastructure.

Calling this bug "flaky tests" is a misleading frame — the tests and their assertions are correct, and the actual defect is that the isolation model assumes single-tenant database ownership per test file while the runtime configuration grants no such isolation.

A single green CI run after applying a fix proves nothing about a race condition, because races are nondeterministic by nature; the fix must be validated by running the parallel configuration repeatedly (multiple CI runs or a `--repeat` loop) before it can be trusted.

The guard that prevents the regression — the `singleFork: true` flag or the `VITEST_POOL_ID`-derived per-worker database naming — should be left in the config with a comment explaining why it exists, so a future "speed up CI" pull request that tries to remove it for performance fails loudly or is caught in review instead of silently reintroducing the exact same race.

CSS-class selectors like `.btn-primary` and structural selectors like `.form-field:nth-child(2) input` are coupled to styling and DOM layout rather than to what the element actually is, so they break on any visual refactor even though the element's behavior hasn't changed.

Role-based selectors bound to accessible intent, such as `getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' })`, survive a visual or layout refactor that class-name or position-based selectors don't, and are the resilient default — a test-id selector is only a fallback when no unique role exists.
The same two selectors for the submit button and password field are copy-pasted across all three test cases, so a single DOM change turns into three separate test breakages instead of one.

A small page object, such as an `OrdersFlowPage` class that owns the selectors and exposes a high-level method like `login(email, password)`, fixes both the duplication and the fragile-selector problem at once — the spec stays about behavior and assertions while the selectors live in exactly one place.

A fixed `page.waitForTimeout(3000)` after submit guesses a constant cost for something Playwright can already detect deterministically: on a slow CI runner it may not be long enough and the test fails for no real reason, while on a fast run it is pure wasted time on every single run.

Replacing the fixed sleep with an auto-waiting assertion like `expect(page.getByTestId('orders-heading')).toBeVisible()` is both faster on the happy path and correct on the slow path, because Playwright's `expect` owns its own timeout and re-checks on a tight loop instead of sleeping blind.

Asserting the exact rendered string "Created at 10:24 AM" can never be deterministic, since it depends on the machine's clock and the seed data's exact creation time — the assertion should target stable content instead, such as an order id, a status badge, or the presence of a timestamp-shaped string rather than its literal wall-clock value.

In a PR review, flakiness issues should be raised before maintainability issues, because flaky tests erode trust in the whole suite before anything else does; ranking findings by blast radius and explaining the mechanism behind each one, rather than just stating the rule, is what makes a review teach the author instead of just flagging nitpicks.

Combining `ADD COLUMN` with a `NOT NULL` constraint and a `DEFAULT` value in one statement forces Postgres to take an `AccessExclusiveLock` and materialize the default into every existing row while verifying the constraint in the same pass, blocking all readers and writers for the duration.

Adding the column as nullable first is metadata-only and near-instant regardless of table size, because Postgres does not need to rewrite existing rows; the `NOT NULL` constraint can then be added later as a separate, cheap verification step once the data is confirmed clean.

A single unbatched `UPDATE` that scans the whole table inside one transaction holds row locks proportional to the number of rows touched, so on a 12-million-row table it holds those locks for minutes against live traffic instead of returning instantly.

Replacing the unbatched `UPDATE` with a batched, idempotent, resumable backfill — chunks of roughly a thousand rows selected by key, with a brief pause between batches — lets live writes and replication interleave between batches instead of being blocked for one long transaction.

`CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` takes a lock for the entire build and blocks writes the whole time, whereas `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` builds the index in a background two-pass process that avoids blocking writers, at the cost of needing to run outside TypeORM's default migration transaction (`transaction = false as const`).

Every one of these lock costs scales with row count, not with the SQL statement itself, so a migration finishing in milliseconds against a 5,000-row staging table proves nothing about how it behaves against a 12-million-row production table — staging passing is not evidence of safety here.

Shipping a migration in the same release as application code that depends on the column it adds (like `AdminGuard` reading `user.role`) breaks rollback: if the migration fails mid-deploy the already-running code expects a column that doesn't exist, and rolling the code back then implicitly forces a database rollback too.

The expand-contract discipline — deploying the schema migration to completion first and only shipping the dependent application code in a following release — keeps the schema a strict superset of every deployed code version, so a code rollback never requires a reverse migration.

Verifying the safe restructuring means watching `pg_locks`/`pg_stat_activity` during a rehearsal against a production-sized copy to confirm no `AccessExclusiveLock` outlives the expand/enforce steps, confirming zero remaining NULLs before enforcing `NOT NULL`, and checking `pg_index.indisvalid` after the concurrent index build to catch a silently failed build.

Docker caches each layer by the content hash of that specific layer's own input, not the Dockerfile as a whole — a layer only stays cached when its own input is byte-for-byte unchanged from the previous build.

Because `COPY . .` is the first COPY instruction in the builder stage, its input is the entire source tree, so editing even a single line in any source file changes that layer's hash and invalidates it.

Layer invalidation cascades downward: once a layer is invalidated, every layer after it in the Dockerfile is invalidated too, so `RUN npm ci` sitting right after `COPY . .` reinstalls dependencies from scratch on every commit even though `package.json` and `package-lock.json` never changed.

Stable-first ordering fixes this: copying `package.json` and `package-lock.json` first and running `npm ci` immediately after ties the install layer's cache key solely to the lockfile's content, so a code-only change no longer touches it.

Only after the install step should the full source be copied with `COPY . .`, followed by `RUN npm run build` — a code-only commit then hits cache on the expensive install layer and only reruns the copy-source and build steps.

A BuildKit cache mount such as `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci` preserves previously downloaded packages even when the lockfile genuinely changes and the install layer legitimately reruns, avoiding a cold re-download from the registry and saving roughly 60-80% of install time on CI runners with no pre-warmed cache.

Pinning the base image to an exact version like `node:20.11.1-alpine` (or a digest) instead of a floating tag such as `20-alpine` prevents the registry from silently publishing a new digest under the same tag and resetting the base-image cache tier without anyone noticing.

After the fix, a code-only rebuild shows the manifest-copy and `npm ci` layers as `CACHED` in the build log, dropping total build time from about 8 minutes to seconds-to-tens-of-seconds, while a rebuild triggered by a genuine lockfile change reruns the install layer but shows no meaningful package-download time because the cache mount serves it.

Feedback latency (time-to-first-signal) matters more than total wall-clock in a CI pipeline; running lint last means the cheapest, most common failure surfaces slowest, at minute ~20-24 instead of within a minute of pushing.

Cheap, deterministic checks like lint should run ahead of expensive, flaky ones like E2E — ordering steps by cost gives fast fail signals without forcing every failure to wait behind the longest suite.

Splitting a single serial job into independent jobs — lint, unit, e2e — triggered by the same event lets the CI platform schedule them onto separate runners in parallel, collapsing wall-clock from the sum of all steps (~25 min) down to roughly the longest leg (~15 min for e2e).
Decoupling the checks into separate jobs also means a flaky e2e rerun no longer forces lint and unit to rerun alongside it, since they are independent rather than sequential steps inside one job.

`actions/setup-node@v4`'s `cache: 'npm'` option (or an explicit `actions/cache@v4` step) keyed on `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')` caches the `~/.npm` store rather than `node_modules` itself, so `npm ci`'s integrity check still runs on install while avoiding a fully cold download every time.

Adding a restore-keys prefix — the cache key string with the trailing hash portion dropped — lets a near-miss, such as a single dependency bump, still restore most of the store instead of falling back to a completely cold install.

Matrixing jobs across multiple Node versions (e.g. 18, 20, 22) multiplies version coverage at roughly the wall-clock cost of a single leg, because matrix legs run in parallel rather than being multiplied serially; the real trade-off is paid in more concurrent runner minutes, not in extra wall-clock time.

A redesign like this should be verified concretely: comparing before/after run durations, timing a deliberately lint-broken commit to confirm a fast first-failure, checking the cache-hit line in the setup-node step's log, and confirming in the Actions tab that the matrix legs actually run concurrently rather than queuing one after another.

A container that builds cleanly, boots cleanly, and serves every GET request while failing only on the first write points to a filesystem-ownership problem inside the image rather than a bug in application logic or a missing directory.

Every `COPY --from=<stage>` instruction in a Dockerfile runs while the build is still executing as root, so any files or directories copied in are owned by root regardless of where a later `USER` instruction appears in the stage.

The `USER` instruction only changes which UID runs the process from that line onward; it does not retroactively change ownership of files or directories that were copied or created earlier in the same build stage.

Reads succeed under a non-root UID because root-owned files and directories grant read and execute permission to "other" by default, so listing or executing them does not require the process to own them.

A write such as `mkdir` or `writeFile` requires write permission on the containing directory, and a root-owned directory with default permissions does not grant that to a non-root UID — which is why the failure surfaces as `EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/reports'` on the first write and not on any read that came before it.

Adding `--chown=1001:1001` to the relevant `COPY --from` instruction, or explicitly creating and `chown`-ing a dedicated writable directory before the `USER` instruction, hands ownership of only the path that needs to be writable to the runtime UID while leaving the rest of the image root-owned.

Running the container as `USER 1001` instead of root exists as a security boundary: a compromised non-root process is limited to whatever paths it owns, whereas a compromised root process could own and modify the entire container filesystem — so removing the `USER` instruction to work around the permission error would eliminate that protection rather than fix the underlying ownership mismatch.

Because a distroless image has no shell to inspect ownership with `stat` or `ls`, verifying the fix requires either overriding the entrypoint to run the image's own `node` binary and call `fs.statSync` on the target directory, or exercising the write endpoint end-to-end after rebuilding and confirming it no longer throws `EACCES`.

Postgres refuses to run `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` inside a transaction block, because the concurrent build needs several independent internal transactions to perform its two-pass scan without holding one long-lived lock — and migration runners such as TypeORM wrap every migration's `up()` in a single transaction by default, which is exactly why the very first deploy attempt fails instantly with that error.

The fix for that first failure is to opt the migration out of the runner's default transaction wrapper (for example setting `transaction = false as const` on the TypeORM migration class), not to retry the same statement as-is.

Disabling the transaction wrapper also strips away the runner's automatic rollback-on-failure safety net for that specific migration, so if the build is interrupted afterward nothing automatically cleans it up.

When a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` build is interrupted mid-way — a deploy timeout, a killed DB connection — Postgres does not roll it back; it leaves the index's catalog entry behind marked invalid, reflected as `pg_index.indisvalid = false`.

An invalid leftover index occupies its name and consumes disk space but is completely ignored by the query planner, which is why the target query is still just as slow even though an index with that name already exists in the catalog.

That same invalid leftover is also why a plain retry of `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_user_email` fails with "relation already exists" — the name is already taken by the broken entry, and issuing the same create statement again cannot repair or replace it.

The correct recovery procedure is to first confirm the index is actually invalid by checking `pg_index.indisvalid` rather than assuming, then drop it (`DROP INDEX`, or `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` to avoid taking a blocking lock during the drop itself), and only then re-run `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` with the transaction wrapper still disabled.

Verification has to go beyond a successful CLI exit code: re-checking `indisvalid = true` after the rebuild and running `EXPLAIN` on the target query confirms the planner is genuinely using the new index, since `CONCURRENTLY` trades a slower two-pass build and no transactional safety net for keeping reads and writes uninterrupted during the build, and that invalid-on-interrupt failure mode needs to be a documented recovery step rather than something the team rediscovers during an incident.

A `deploy` job with no `needs: [lint, test]` and no `if:` condition runs in parallel with the `test` job on every trigger, including pushes on a PR branch — a failing test does nothing to stop it because no dependency links the two jobs.

Adding `needs: [lint, test]` together with `if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` is what turns tests merely passing into tests being required before deploy runs, and it also keeps PR branches from ever triggering a deploy at all.

Explicitly echoing a secret's value (`echo ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}`) can still leak it into the run log, because GitHub's log masking only redacts output that matches the secret's own literal characters — an intentional echo of the value defeats that protection rather than being caught by it.

The exposure from printing a secret in a log is worse on a workflow that can run against fork pull requests, since the trust boundary for who can trigger the job and see its output is different there.
A secret should be referenced only inside a step's `env:` or `with:` block and passed to the tool that needs it directly, never written out through a `run:` shell command.

Caching `node_modules` directly instead of the package manager's own store (such as `~/.npm`) means that on a cache hit, `npm ci` never gets the chance to re-verify the installed tree against `package-lock.json`, so a stale or corrupted cache entry can be silently reused.

Caching the package manager's store keyed on the lockfile hash while still running `npm ci` on every job keeps both properties intact: the store makes the install fast, and the install step itself is what re-verifies integrity against the lockfile.

Pushing every image as `:latest` leaves production pointing at a moving target with no commit-SHA-pinned reference to roll back to; tagging the image with `${{ github.sha }}` and retaining previous tags gives rollback a concrete target to point at.

A senior-style PR review orders findings by blast radius rather than by the order they appear in the file, and separates must-fix-before-merge issues (an ungated deploy path, a leaked secret) from lower-severity mechanical nits (cache correctness, tag mutability).

Proving a new deploy gate actually works means pushing a commit with an intentionally failing test and confirming the Actions run shows `deploy` skipped by `needs:` and never starting — not started-then-failed, which would indicate the gate isn't wired correctly.

Hand-assembling the response envelope inside each handler duplicates the contract once per handler, so every new handler is another chance for the success and error shapes to drift apart — which has already happened here: one handler's success body includes `timestamp` while the other's doesn't, and one names the payload `data` while the other calls it `result`.

Returning `res.status(200)` from inside a catch block hides a real failure behind a success status code, so both the client and any monitoring or alerting keyed on HTTP status read a thrown error as if the request succeeded.

Collapsing every caught error into one hard-coded status (such as 500) erases the distinction between an expected domain error — like a referenced resource not being found — and a genuine server fault, so a case that should surface as 404 instead reads as an indistinguishable internal failure.

Forwarding a caught exception's raw `.message` straight into the JSON response body leaks internal implementation detail (driver, ORM, or other low-level error text) to external clients instead of returning a controlled, generic message.

The fix is not to patch each handler's shaping logic but to remove response construction from handlers entirely: a handler should return plain business data on success or throw a semantic domain exception (e.g. `NotFoundException`, `BadRequestException`) on failure, and do nothing else.

Success-response shaping belongs in exactly one place — a single global interceptor — so that every route in the API shares one canonical envelope shape instead of each handler re-implementing it slightly differently.

Error normalization belongs in exactly one place — a single global exception filter — which can branch on known versus unknown exception types, attach fields like details/timestamp/path, and fall back to a generic message for anything not explicitly recognized, so leaking internal detail becomes structurally impossible rather than a per-handler discipline.

Verifying this kind of centralization calls for contract-level tests rather than manual inspection: asserting every route's success response shares the same root keys, that a thrown domain not-found exception produces a 404 in the standard error envelope, and that an unrecognized error degrades to a generic 500 envelope whose message contains none of the original internal error text.

Applying pagination by slicing an already-fetched array in application memory after an unbounded `find()`/`SELECT *` still returns correct page contents for every request — the output looking right is exactly why this bug survives code review even though the entire table is read every time.

When a repository call carries no where/skip/take criteria, the data source returns every row in the table before any slicing happens; the cost is O(total rows) for I/O, ORM hydration, and JSON serialization on each request, independent of the requested page size — page 1 with limit 10 against 2 rows or 2,000,000 rows does the identical 'fetch everything' work.

Because this per-request cost scales with table size, p95 latency and memory climb roughly linearly as the table grows, and N concurrent requests each hold their own full in-memory copy of the table at once, multiplying the cost under load.

The fix is to push `page`/`limit` down into the query itself — `repo.find({ skip: (page - 1) * limit, take: limit })` or a query builder's `.skip().take()` — which compiles to a SQL `OFFSET`/`LIMIT` clause so the database performs the windowing and only one page of rows ever leaves the DB, crosses the network, or gets serialized.

Pushing pagination into the query changes only what happens between the repository call and the database — the controller's response shape and the contract given to the client stay identical, so the optimization is invisible to callers.

Computing `skip: (page - 1) * limit` as safe arithmetic depends entirely on the query DTO's `@Type(() => Number)`, `@IsInt`, `@Min(1)`, and default values already guaranteeing that `page`/`limit` are real, bounded, positive integers by the time they reach the service.

If raw, unvalidated query-string values fed that same offset formula instead, a non-numeric `page` would produce `NaN`, and a zero or negative `page` would produce a negative offset — which several databases either reject or silently treat as 'no offset,' leaking rows or erroring deep in the DB layer instead of failing cleanly with a 400 at the boundary.

Verifying the fix means diffing the returned rows for the same page/limit combinations before and after the change (contents must be identical), then confirming the win through query logging showing a single `SELECT ... LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2` instead of an unbounded `SELECT *`, or through load testing showing latency flatten instead of scale with table size, while re-confirming the boundary still rejects an invalid `page` with 400.

Offset-based pagination itself degrades at very deep pages because the database still has to walk past every skipped row before returning results; keyset/cursor pagination — filtering by `WHERE id > lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT n` — avoids that cost by never asking the database to scan past rows it isn't returning.

Calling `SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config)` inside a request handler means the full controller/DTO metadata scan and OpenAPI document assembly reruns on every single hit to that route, which is why an idle service shows rising CPU the moment something polls the endpoint repeatedly.

The generated OpenAPI document is a deterministic function of the code currently deployed in the running process — two requests handled by the same process, with no code change between them, can never produce a different document, so recomputing it per request just recreates a byte-identical artifact N times.

Because the expensive scan-and-assemble step yields the same output for the lifetime of a process, that work belongs at startup (or memoized on the first hit) rather than inside the request path; after that, serving the spec is nothing more than returning an already-built object.

The fix is to call `createDocument` exactly once during bootstrap, hold the resulting document, and have the route return that held object instead of rebuilding it — moving one function call out of the request handler removes the entire per-request scan.

Using `SwaggerModule.setup("swagger", app, document)` instead of hand-wiring the JSON route lets one generated document back both the human-readable UI at `/swagger` and the raw JSON at `/swagger-json`, so there is one artifact serving multiple surfaces rather than duplicated generation logic.

The document only changes when the code changes, and a code change requires a new build and a fresh process that runs bootstrap again — so generating the spec at startup is exactly as fresh as generating it per request, just at a fraction of the cost, which is the direct answer to "but what if the spec needs to change?"

There is no runtime scenario where a live, already-booted process needs to serve a newer spec than the one produced when it started, since nothing about its own routes or DTOs can mutate without a redeploy.

Correctness of the fix is verified by checking that the `/swagger-json` response body is byte-identical before and after the change, that latency and CPU flatten to the cost of serving a cached object even under continuous polling, and that after an actual code change plus redeploy the served document reflects the new schema — proving the switch to startup generation never sacrificed freshness.
In an UpdateUserDto where every field is marked optional, a client that omits a field causes that field to arrive at the handler as `undefined`, not as something the handler can treat as "skip this."

Assigning a payload field directly onto the entity row without checking whether it was actually present applies full-replace semantics to a route meant to only touch what changed — the omitted field gets overwritten with `undefined`, and the ORM persists that as `null`, wiping previously stored data.

PUT and PATCH differ in write scope: PUT is a full replacement where the client sends the complete representation and the server can assign every field directly, while PATCH is a partial update where the server must write only the fields present in the payload and leave everything else untouched.

The fix is a per-field presence check before assignment — e.g. `if (payload.name !== undefined) row.name = payload.name` — so a field absent from the payload keeps its previously stored value instead of being cleared.

Adding a "keep the old value if the field is absent" fallback to a genuine PUT handler is the mirror-image bug: it lets omitted fields silently survive a request that is contractually supposed to overwrite the whole resource, breaking PUT's replace-everything guarantee.

Verifying the fix requires checking both directions independently: PATCH with a partial body leaves the untouched field unchanged, PUT with a full body overwrites every field, and resending that same PUT payload again converges the resource to the same state, which is the idempotency property both PUT and PATCH are expected to have.

The presence-check strategy is representation-dependent: an `!== undefined`/null check works when the language distinguishes "absent" from "a real value," but in languages where an absent field arrives as a zero-value (e.g. an empty string in Go), the same strategy needs a different signal — a pointer type or an explicit presence map — to distinguish "not sent" from "sent as empty."

A plain undefined/null presence check cannot distinguish "field was never sent" from "field was sent as null/empty specifically to clear it" — supporting an intentional clear operation requires an extra signal beyond simple presence checking, such as a sentinel value or a separate "fields to clear" list.

Two error shapes coming out of the same API for what is conceptually the same kind of failure (an error) usually means two different code paths are handling errors, not one - the discriminator is a property of how each error is routed, not randomness or client-side parsing.

A parameterized `@Catch(HttpException)` scopes a filter to only intercept exceptions that are instances of that specific type - it does not act as a global safety net for everything an application can throw.

A plain `throw new Error("boom")` is not an instance of `HttpException`, so it never matches a filter scoped with `@Catch(HttpException)` and is never routed to that filter at all, regardless of the filter being registered globally.

An exception that bypasses a type-scoped filter falls straight through to the framework's own built-in default exception handler, which builds its own response body in a different shape and, depending on configuration, can surface the raw error message or a stack trace directly to the client.

Making the catch registration unconditional (a parameterless `@Catch()`) turns the filter into a true catch-all so no exception type can structurally bypass it, closing the gap that let plain runtime errors slip through.

Once the filter is a catch-all, it must branch internally: when the caught value is an `HttpException`, its real status and message are preserved and returned as before; otherwise the response is hardcoded to a generic 500 with a generic message, while the actual exception and its stack trace are logged server-side only, never included in the response body.

An exception filter functions as the single border deciding what error information leaves the system, so preventing leaks has to be a structural property of that boundary's scope rather than a hope that every handler always throws a recognized, deliberately-shaped error.

Correctness after the fix is confirmed by three checks together: the previously-leaking endpoint now returns the same envelope shape with a generic message and no internal string; a genuine `HttpException` such as a 404 still returns its original status and details unchanged; and the real error plus its stack trace still appears in server logs, showing nothing was silently swallowed - only hidden from the client.

Copying an entire raw request body directly onto a persistence entity (mass assignment) lets a client set fields the API never intended to accept — for example flipping an `isAdmin` flag to true through one extra key in the payload — which is a privilege-escalation vulnerability, not a cosmetic issue.

The fix for mass assignment is a declared boundary contract — a DTO listing only the fields the endpoint is meant to accept — enforced as an allowlist (e.g. a validation pipe configured with `whitelist`/`forbidNonWhitelisted`) so unknown fields are stripped or the whole request is rejected before it ever reaches the persistence layer.

Reusing the persistence entity itself as the input type merges the wire contract with the storage shape, so any column added later for internal bookkeeping (like an admin flag) automatically becomes a client-writable input field.

Manual inline validation — scattered if-statements invented per handler — drifts over time, tends to miss real rules such as email format checking, and produces inconsistent, ad hoc error messages across different endpoints.

Declarative validation (decorators such as `@IsEmail`, `@MinLength`, `@Min`) combined with one global validation layer applied to every route produces consistent, structured error responses and removes the need to hand-roll checks per handler.

A nested object field, such as an address, is persisted with no deep validation unless the contract explicitly declares nested validation for it, so an invalid nested value is silently stored instead of surfacing an error with a specific field path like `address.zip`.

A query parameter that looks numeric is still a string on the wire; without explicit type coercion, a comparison such as `age >= minAge` compares a number against a string and can silently misbehave instead of throwing an error.

Verifying a fix for these problems means confirming that an unexpected extra field is rejected or stripped rather than persisted, that a bad nested field returns an error carrying its correct nested path, that a numeric-looking query parameter now compares correctly, and that a previously valid payload still behaves exactly as before.

In a prompt-safety pipeline, redacting PII before the injection scanner runs wastes redaction work on prompts that are about to be blocked anyway, and it makes the block decision incidentally depend on the redaction step having executed first — a dependency that should not exist. The injection scan should run first, against the raw prompt, before any redaction happens.

Wrapping the injection-scanner call in a try/catch that logs a warning and then calls the LLM provider anyway on any exception is a fail-open design: the exact moment the scanner is broken or throws is the moment the entire safety gate silently becomes a pass-through, forwarding the raw, unredacted prompt straight to the provider.

Of the violations in such a pipeline, the fail-open catch around the scanner is the most severe because it is silent and total — any runtime exception converts the whole gate into a bypass, and a log line like "scanner failed, continuing" reads as a benign warning rather than signaling that the safety layer just failed, so no one gets paged for it.

Because redaction runs before the scan, a scanner failure forwards a prompt that has already been redacted, which makes the response look "safe-ish" even though the actual security control — injection detection — never ran at all; the two violations compound each other.

Writing the full raw prompt into the audit log when a request is blocked, "for debugging," copies any PII that prompt contains into every log aggregator and retention policy that engineers with log access can reach — a second, unintended exposure of the exact data the pipeline exists to protect, even though nothing left the process to an external provider.

A fail-closed fix means any exception during the scan step must result in a blocked response (or be rethrown to a global filter that returns an error status), never a fallthrough to the provider call — "I don't know if this is safe" has to be treated the same as "this is unsafe," not the same as "this is safe."

Audit logging on a blocked decision should record only the decision and evidence — such as the matched finding kinds — never the raw prompt text; on a successful forward, only the already-redacted prompt should be logged, never the original raw input.

Proving such a fix requires tests showing: a prompt containing both an injection phrase and PII is blocked with zero calls to the provider and no redaction warning, proving order; forcing the scanner to throw results in a blocked response and never a forwarded one, proving fail-closed behavior; and captured log output for both a block and a forward never contains the raw PII substring from the input, proving the log boundary holds.

Selecting every row from `documents` with no `ORDER BY` and no `LIMIT` forces the full table — id, content, and every embedding vector — to be pulled out of Postgres and shipped over the wire on each retrieval call.

Computing `cosineSimilarity` in application code once per row is an O(n) scan across the entire corpus for every single query, and sorting all of those scored rows in memory before slicing the top 3 wastes work on rows that get thrown away.

This pattern is invisible at a handful of seed documents because the data volume and scan cost are both trivial, but it degrades badly as the corpus grows into the hundreds of thousands of chunks — the LLM call is not the bottleneck, the network transfer and the app-side scan are.

The first-stage fix is to move the nearest-neighbour search into the database itself: query with `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT $2` using pgvector's cosine-distance operator, so Postgres does the ranking and only the top-k rows ever cross the wire.

The similarity-to-score conversion (`1 - distance`) and the `SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` filter should still be applied, but only to the k rows the database returns, not to the whole corpus — the app-side `cosineSimilarity` and `parseVectorLiteral` helpers drop out of the request path entirely once the query does the work.

An approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat should only be introduced once the exact in-database scan itself becomes the bottleneck at very large scale — it is a second-stage optimization, not an automatic first move.

Adding an ANN index trades exactness for speed: the neighbours returned become approximate rather than guaranteed top-k, so the recall loss versus the latency gain is a judged trade-off rather than a free win.

Verifying the change means measuring p95 query latency before and after at a realistic corpus size, running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm the query plan actually uses the index once one exists, checking retrieval quality hasn't silently regressed by comparing approximate results against an exact scan on a sample of queries, and re-running the grounded and fallback end-to-end flows to confirm answers still cite the right chunks.

User-perceived latency in a streaming response is governed by time-to-first-token, not total generation time — the two are independent, and a fix that shortens total generation time without moving the first byte earlier does nothing for perceived latency.

Setting `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and shaping each event correctly makes an endpoint look like it streams, but the actual guarantee of streaming is that bytes cross the socket as each token is produced — correct framing and early delivery are separate properties, and only the second one fixes a blank-screen wait.

Pushing each formatted token into an in-memory array (or string) inside a `for await` loop and calling `res.write` only once after the loop exits collapses time-to-first-token to the full generation duration, because nothing reaches the client until every token has already been generated.

A client's request status can flip to 'streaming' the instant the HTTP response opens, independent of whether the server has written any data yet — so status alone does not prove data is arriving, and a blank screen with status already 'streaming' points at server-side buffering rather than a client-side issue.

Fixing the in-memory accumulation bug is not sufficient on its own: headers set via `setHeader` are not guaranteed to reach the client until the first write or an explicit flush, so calling `res.flushHeaders()` right after setting headers is needed for the client to see the connection open before the first token arrives.

Without a `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` response header (and, behind nginx specifically, `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), an intermediate reverse proxy or CDN is free to buffer correctly-flushed per-token writes and release them together later — so the server-side fix and the anti-buffering header are two independent, both-required fixes for the same symptom.

The correct fix moves the write inside the loop: each token is written and flushed to the response the moment it is produced, with no accumulating array or string kept — only a running counter is needed to report the total token count in the terminal 'done' event.

Verifying a streaming fix requires more than reading the code: asserting that response output grows while status is still 'streaming', measuring time-to-first-token before and after the fix, and re-running that check through the actual reverse proxy or CDN in front of the service — since a local request bypasses proxy-level buffering and cannot reveal it.

An SSE streaming handler has two independent lifecycles running side by side — the HTTP connection to the client and the token-generation loop pulling from the provider — and nothing links them unless code explicitly bridges the two.

An AbortController that is instantiated and correctly threaded into a provider's streamCompletion(...) call is not sufficient on its own; the controller only stops generation once something actually calls .abort() on it.

A framework does not automatically translate a client-side disconnect (closing the tab, tearing down a fetch) into an abort signal — that translation requires an explicit listener such as req.on("close", () => abortController.abort()).

Without a close-listener wired to the abort controller, abortController.signal.aborted never flips to true, so a for-await loop over the provider stream keeps pulling and writing tokens until the provider naturally finishes, even though the client already left.

Writing SSE frames to a connection nobody is reading and letting generation run to completion after a disconnect means that, with a real provider, the full completion still gets billed even though the response is discarded.

The fix requires two things together: registering an abort trigger on the connection's close event (or an equivalent request-scoped cancellation token/context the platform ties to the connection) and continuing to pass that same abort signal into the provider call exactly as before.

Checking abortController.signal.aborted before each write inside the streaming loop lets the loop break out immediately on cancellation rather than waiting for the next token from the provider, and that same check should guard against sending a terminal "done" frame after an abort.

Correct verification for this kind of fix is starting a stream, aborting after the first token, and confirming the server log stops at a low token count with an aborted/warning line and no "done" event — instead of continuing on to the full token count as if the client never left.

pgvector's `<=>` cosine-distance operator returns a value where a SMALLER number means the two vectors are more alike (0 for identical direction), which is the opposite of what a similarity score means.
Similarity is derived from distance as `1 - distance`, so it points the opposite direction from distance: a LARGER similarity value means more relevant, not less.

In `searchSimilar`, the SELECT projects `embedding <=> $1::vector AS score`, handing `score` the raw distance value, while `.filter((chunk) => chunk.score >= SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD)` is written as if `score` were a similarity — comparing a distance with `>=` against a similarity threshold inverts relevance.

This single inversion produces both symptoms at once: an on-topic chunk with a tiny distance (e.g. ~0.05) fails `0.05 >= 0.3`, gets filtered out, leaves zero chunks, and forces the `grounded=false` fallback even though the right document was retrieved.

An off-topic, near-orthogonal chunk with a large distance (e.g. ~0.6) passes `0.6 >= 0.3`, survives the filter, gets fed into the augmented prompt, and causes the LLM to answer confidently while citing an unrelated document.

`ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector` ranks strictly by ascending distance, so the closest chunk is always first before `LIMIT` cuts the top-k — the ordering logic is correct and is not the source of either bug.

The fix restores the missing distance-to-similarity conversion, e.g. rewriting the projection as `1 - (embedding <=> $1::vector) AS score` inside the same SQL query with no application-layer change needed, while the `ORDER BY` clause and the `>=` comparison stay untouched since only the meaning of `score` needs to change.

Proving the fix closes both bug reports requires an e2e regression pair rather than a single test: a known on-topic query must return `grounded: true` with the expected citation, and a known off-topic query must return `grounded: false` with empty citations, since testing only one direction would not catch the inversion resurfacing.

A guard that protects an expensive call must run as an admission check before that call executes, not as a report computed after the call already happened - a check placed after the provider call has already spent the money it was supposed to prevent spending.

In this handler, `this.cost.priceOf(result)` runs and `this.spentDollars` is updated right after `completion.complete(prompt)` returns, and only afterward is `spentDollars` compared against `budgetLimitDollars` - so the provider call and its cost are always paid before the budget is checked, guaranteeing the cap is overshot by at least one full paid request every time it is crossed.

Because the rejection only fires after the spend already happened, the caller whose request actually pushed spending over the budget still gets served in full; only their next request receives the 429 - enforcement lags one request behind the violation it is meant to prevent.

The fix is to turn the budget check into an admission gate: read the accumulated spend, compare it to the limit, and throw `429 BUDGET_EXCEEDED` (with the spent and limit figures in the response body) before `completion.complete` is ever invoked, the same way the rate-limit check already runs ahead of the handler's real work.

`remainingRequests` is a single field on the service instance with no `userId` anywhere near it, so every caller shares the same counter - one user issuing enough requests can exhaust the allowance meant for the entire user base, leaving everyone else rate-limited by someone else's traffic.

Per-user rate limiting requires keying the counter by `userId` (e.g. a `Map<string, Bucket>` token bucket); once the service runs more than one replica, that state can no longer live on `this` - each instance would keep its own counter and silently multiply the real limit by the replica count, so the bucket state has to move to a shared store like Redis with an atomic refill-and-consume operation.

`spentDollars` accumulates as a floating-point dollar amount on every call (`+= costDollars`), and floating-point addition of many small fractional values drifts away from the true total over time, so the number the budget guard compares against the limit can quietly disagree with what was actually billed.

Money should be accumulated as an integer unit such as micro-USD (`spentMicroUsd += 660`) rather than a float, since integer arithmetic has no rounding drift and keeps the figure the budget guard reads and the figure the cost log reports as one consistent, drift-free source of truth.

A persisted-query hash is only meaningful as a content identifier - the hash-to-query mapping is trustworthy only when the server itself proves hash equals SHA-256(query) at registration time, rather than accepting whatever pairing a client asserts.

In this implementation, the register endpoint calls `store.set(body.hash, body.query)` directly on unverified client input; because registration now happens outside Apollo's `persistedQueries.cache.set`, Apollo's own built-in hash-matches-query verification never runs at all.

Since the store never checks that the hash matches the query, any client can register an attacker-chosen query under a hash the legitimate app is already known to send hash-only, overwriting or seeding that exact cache entry.

Once a malicious pair is registered, every subsequent hash-only request from real clients - including the official app itself - resolves to and executes the attacker's query instead of the original one, turning a bandwidth optimization into a remote-injection primitive that redirects an entire population of well-behaved callers without touching their code.

The minimum fix is to recompute `sha256(query)` on every store write and reject the request (4xx) when it doesn't equal the supplied hash, which restores exactly the guarantee Apollo's built-in persisted-query cache already provides, making the custom register endpoint unnecessary in favor of the standard protocol.

A stronger posture removes client-driven registration entirely: a build-time trusted-documents allowlist generates the hash-to-query manifest from the client's real query set ahead of time, so the server only ever executes pre-approved hashes and never accepts a query string from a request.

The store backing this registry is an unbounded Map with no TTL or eviction, so junk registrations let it grow forever with no way to bound memory or age out stale entries, compounding the security risk with a resource-growth issue.

Correctness here is proven by tests showing a mismatched hash/query pair is rejected without altering the existing entry for that hash, a legitimate register-then-hash-only round trip still resolves, and repeated junk registrations cannot evict or replace a known-good mapping.

A batching data loader only collapses keys that get registered within the same event-loop tick (the batch dispatch window) into one call; once that window closes, any further `load()` calls open a new window of their own.

Awaiting a `load()` call inside a `for...of` loop fully pauses that iteration until the promise resolves, so the next iteration's `load()` call happens on a later tick — this closes the batch window after exactly one key every time, even though the loader's batch function and scope are configured correctly.

N single-key batch lines in the data-source log (`[BATCH] ... IN ('<one-id>')` repeated N times) instead of one combined multi-key line is the fingerprint of broken batching — it is N+1 in disguise, N sequential round-trips happening despite a batching loader being wired up.

The root cause lives in the calling code's control flow, not in the loader's configuration: the loader itself, its batch function, and its request scope are not the source of the bug, so 'fixing' the loader's setup would not resolve the slowdown.

The fix is to register every `load()` call before awaiting any of them, so all keys land in the same tick: mapping over the collection to start every `load()` synchronously and only then awaiting them together (e.g. with a single combined wait over all the pending calls) lets the loader batch them into one `IN (...)` query.

Turning the related field into its own field resolver that returns the loader's pending call directly, without an `await` inside that resolver, is the more idiomatic fix — the GraphQL engine itself invokes that field once per parent within the same execution tick, so all the resulting `load()` calls naturally land in the same batch window without any manual `Promise.all`.

The loader's per-request cache deduplicates a key that gets loaded twice within the same request, but that is a separate mechanism from batching by width; since every key in this scenario is unique, the cache cannot mask or fix a sequential-await bug like this one.

Proving the fix requires counting batch-log lines for the same nested query before and after (N single-key lines collapsing to one multi-key line) and re-measuring latency against the size of the parent list (linear growth flattening out), then locking in a regression test that asserts exactly one batch-log line per relation per request so the sequential-await bug cannot silently return.

APQ's payoff is amortisation: after a one-time round trip where the client registers the full query and receives a hash back, every subsequent call sends only a 64-character SHA-256 hash instead of the full query text.

That payoff only holds if a registered hash means something the whole fleet agrees on. `PersistedQueryStore.store` is a plain `Map` living in a single NestJS process's heap, so a hash set by one replica is invisible to the `Map` instances running in the other replicas.

With 4 replicas behind round-robin routing and no shared cache, a hash registered on one replica is recognized only when a later request happens to land back on that same replica - about 1 in 4 times - while the other 3 in 4 requests still return PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND. That is the arithmetic source of the observed ~75% miss rate.
A rolling restart clears the in-memory `Map` on whichever pod cycles, erasing every hash that pod had learned and forcing a fresh miss storm across the fleet as clients re-register from scratch.

The fix has to match the registry's storage to the unit of deployment (the whole fleet) rather than the unit of a single process. Apollo Server's `persistedQueries.cache` accepts any object implementing `get`/`set`/`delete`, so the storage backend is a drop-in swap that requires no resolver code changes.

Backing the registry with a shared store such as Redis (for example `apollo-server-cache-redis`'s `RedisCache`), combined with a TTL so the registry doesn't grow unbounded, makes a registration visible to every replica and lets it survive any single pod restarting.

For first-party clients, generating a hash-to-query manifest at build time and shipping it with the client (trusted documents) goes further: the server never accepts an arbitrary client-supplied registration at all, which removes both the miss storm and the open registration attack surface in one move.

Validating the fix requires more than reading the diff: the `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate should fall to near zero at steady state, average request payload should shrink to hash-size, a rolling-restart soak should confirm registrations survive pod churn, and the Redis-backed store itself should be load-tested so its added network hop doesn't become the new bottleneck.

DataLoader's batch function must return a result array of the exact same length and order as the keys array it receives, because DataLoader hands result[i] back to whichever caller invoked load(keys[i]) — matching happens purely by index, never by inspecting the content of the returned rows.

Grouping a flat SQL result set by iterating the rows themselves — rather than iterating the original keys array — produces an output ordered by whatever sequence the rows first appeared in, since an unordered SQL IN clause never guarantees it will return rows in the same order as the ids that were passed in.

An author with zero books contributes no group to a row-order-based grouping, so it doesn't just occupy the wrong slot itself — it silently deletes one array slot and shifts the position of every subsequent author's group by one index, compounding the misalignment for everything after it.

The batched query itself is correct and genuinely avoids N+1, which means this class of bug can hide behind SQL that looks completely fine — the defect lives entirely in how the batch function reshapes its query results back into the keys' order, not in the query.

The symptom is intermittent rather than constant because the misalignment only manifests when the database's row-return order diverges from the requested keys' order or a zero-books author sits among the batch; whenever the two orders happen to coincide, the mismatched code produces correct-looking output by coincidence.

A single-author query never exposes this bug because batching only ever contains one key, so there is nothing for that one result to be out of order relative to — it always lands at index 0 regardless of how the batch function grouped it, making single-key tests a red herring that masks the real defect.

The correct fix is to build an intermediate map keyed by each id while iterating the rows, then derive the final result by mapping over the original keys array and looking up each key in that map, falling back to an empty array for keys with no matching rows — this guarantees position i always corresponds to keys[i] and makes missing entries explicit instead of silently absent.

Verifying the fix requires asserting that every returned child record's foreign key matches its parent's id in a nested query, plus a regression fixture where an entity with zero related rows is sandwiched between two entities that do have rows, since that specific arrangement is what exposes an index shift.

`new PubSub()` from `graphql-subscriptions` creates an in-process object — `publish()` only reaches `asyncIterator`s that were instantiated inside the same running Node process, not across any process boundary.
On a single dev instance there is only one process, so the mutation's `publish` call and the subscription's `asyncIterator` are always the same object — every event is delivered with no exceptions.

Running the service as 3 replicas behind a load balancer means each replica boots its own copy of the service with its own private, unshared `PubSub` instance in memory — there are effectively three separate topics that happen to share the same string name.

A subscriber's WebSocket is a long-lived connection pinned to whichever replica accepted the upgrade, while each `createPost` mutation is a separate HTTP/WS request the load balancer is free to route to any replica independently.

An event reaches a given subscriber only when the replica that ran the mutation happens to be the same replica the subscriber's WebSocket is connected to; with 3 replicas and roughly uniform routing that coincidence happens about 1 in 3 times, exactly matching the reported symptom.

Sticky WebSocket sessions do not fix this bug: stickiness only pins the subscriber's connection to one replica, but does nothing to the mutation request, which remains a separate call the load balancer can still send to any replica.

The correct fix is to replace the in-memory `PubSub` with an adapter backed by an external shared bus — such as `graphql-redis-subscriptions`'s `RedisPubSub` — so that `publish` and every replica's `asyncIterator` all read from and write to the same external topic regardless of which replica handled the mutation.

The fix can be verified by running 2+ instances locally, opening a subscription against one instance while firing mutations against a different instance, and confirming every event still arrives exactly once with no duplicates once all replicas share the same external bus.

In a partial-update mutation, an absent field must leave the stored value untouched, a field sent as explicit null is a deliberate clear, and a field sent with a real value overwrites the old one — these are three distinct client intents the merge logic has to tell apart.

The nullish coalescing operator (`??`) cannot distinguish "field omitted" from "field sent as explicit null", since both are nullish — `input.publishedYear ?? existing.publishedYear` falls back to the existing value in either case.

Because of that collapse, a client can never actually clear a nullable field like `publishedYear` through this mutation, even though the field is declared nullable in the schema specifically so it can be cleared.

The correct fix is to branch on whether the key is present in the input (for example `'publishedYear' in input` or `input.publishedYear !== undefined`) rather than on whether its value is null: an absent key leaves the existing value untouched, while a present key — including an explicit null — overwrites with whatever the client sent.

`archiveBook` mutates the in-memory store yet is registered with `@Query` instead of `@Mutation`; query operation types are the part of the GraphQL contract that execution engines and clients are permitted to parallelize, prefetch, and cache.

Hiding a side effect inside a query field means it can fire more than once for a single client intent, or race against another field resolving in the same request, because the query contract carries no guarantee of single, serial execution.
Registering the operation as `@Mutation` instead restores the GraphQL guarantee that mutation fields run serially and are never cached or speculatively re-executed.

Locking in the corrected contract needs regression tests covering all three cases: an explicit null persists as null, an omitted field keeps the prior value, and calling a query-type field twice back-to-back leaves the store's state identical both times.

A guard that compares each incoming refund amount against the full captured amount in isolation, without subtracting already-succeeded refunds, lets multiple partial refunds each pass individually while their sum exceeds the captured total.

Three sequential refund requests, each for 60% of a captured amount, all pass an `amount > intent.amount` check because the check is evaluated against the static captured amount rather than what remains after prior successful refunds — the order ends up refunded 180% against 100% captured.

The correct guard recomputes remaining-refundable as the captured amount minus the sum of already-succeeded refunds pulled from the ledger, on every request, so a running total can never cross the captured amount no matter how many partial requests arrive.

Service-side idempotency only protects replays that reach the point where the key gets persisted to the index; a crash between the gateway call succeeding and that write leaves a retry with the same key invisible to the check, so the retry reaches the gateway again as a brand-new refund.

Forwarding the same idempotency key to the payment gateway call closes the crash-then-retry gap, because the gateway's own idempotency map then recognizes the repeated key and returns the original result instead of processing a second real refund.

Two-layer idempotency requires both layers to carry the key: the service layer dedups requests it has already recorded, and the gateway layer dedups calls it has already processed — guarding only one layer leaves the window between "gateway call succeeded" and "record persisted" unprotected.

Money operations sent over HTTP are not retry-safe by default; each idempotency or validation guard only covers the boundary it actually checks, so a fix touching just one layer still allows a duplicate charge or over-refund through the other layer's gap.

Two concrete tests confirm the fix holds: a sequence of partial refunds that sums past the captured amount must reject exactly the request that crosses the limit, and replaying the same idempotency key on an already-succeeded refund must return the identical refund record while the gateway shows exactly one refund was ever created for that key.

Running the confirmation email and fulfillment notification synchronously before the response is returned pushes total handler time past the payment gateway's delivery timeout; under at-least-once delivery semantics, the gateway reads a missed timeout as failure and redelivers the same webhook event.

Each redelivery re-enters the exact same slow synchronous path, adding more load onto an endpoint that is already struggling — the rising p99 latency and the pile of duplicate deliveries are not two separate symptoms but one self-amplifying feedback loop.

An idempotency check keyed on the event id stops the ledger transition from being re-applied on a duplicate delivery, but it does not stop a retry from re-paying the cost of the slow email and fulfillment calls or from occupying another request slot — deduplication alone cannot stop the retry storm.

The minimal work that must complete before the response leaves the handler is: verify the webhook signature, check idempotency by event id, and durably apply the ledger transition — nothing else belongs on that synchronous path.

Sending the confirmation email and notifying the fulfillment service are slow, non-critical-path operations that can be deferred to run after the 200 is returned (for example via a queue or background job), so their latency no longer counts against the gateway's timeout.

The 200 response may only be sent after the ledger transition has been durably persisted; acknowledging first and persisting second opens a window where a crash between the two loses the event permanently, since the gateway never redelivers a webhook it already received a 2xx for. Shortening the synchronous path does not remove the need for the idempotency guard — retries arriving during the transition window still have to be caught by that same check.

The contract that makes deferring the email and fulfillment work safe is that the gateway only needs confirmation the event was received and durably stored, not that it was fully processed end to end; that distinction is what separates a legitimate optimization from a correctness shortcut.

Confirming the fix worked requires checking that p99 ack latency stays under the gateway's timeout under load, replaying duplicate deliveries in a chaos test to confirm the ledger transition applies exactly once, and killing the process between the ack and the deferred job to confirm the durably recorded event lets the email and fulfillment work resume instead of being silently dropped.

A full-history join re-walked on every call makes cost scale with total ledger size rather than with how much activity happened between requests — a dashboard polling this endpoint every few seconds re-fetches and re-sums every intent's refunds from scratch even though only a handful of payments and refunds occurred since the previous poll.

Maintaining a per-intent totalRefunded as a stored running counter, updated in the same write path that flips a refund to Succeeded, replaces an O(intents x refunds) re-filter-and-reduce with a simple field read; keeping the counter rebuildable from the ledger via a periodic reconciliation job means a bug in the counter self-heals instead of becoming a silent, permanent lie in the report.

Caching the whole report as a versioned snapshot and invalidating it the instant a payment or refund write lands turns repeated full joins into a single reused computation, trading a few seconds of staleness for eliminating redundant work — an acceptable trade because the consumer is a dashboard poll, not a strict real-time feed.

Scoping the report by settlement period narrows the initial payment scan to one window instead of the entire ledger's history, since reconciliation is naturally periodic work and its cost should track the period being reconciled rather than the full lifetime of the ledger.

Across every optimization strategy, totalRefunded must keep counting only refunds with status Succeeded and every monetary sum must stay in integer cents with no floating-point rounding introduced — these correctness constraints cannot be relaxed just because the computation path changed.

ReconciliationService has to remain strictly read-only no matter how it's optimized; none of incremental aggregates, caching, or period scoping should turn it into a place that writes a corrected netAmount or any other figure back onto a payment record.

Because this report serves a periodic audit dashboard rather than a real-time feed, trading a bounded amount of staleness for much less repeated work — via caching or period scoping — is the right default, and full incremental real-time accuracy is only worth reaching for when a consumer genuinely can't tolerate any staleness.
