A Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) keeps its members ordered strictly by their numeric score inside an internal skip list, and ZREVRANGE simply walks that skip list from the high end to the low end.

Because ZREVRANGE has no concept of "recency" on its own, the order it returns is entirely determined by whatever value was written as the score at insert time — if that value doesn't represent time, the output doesn't represent time either.

In seedTimeline, the score passed to zadd is `rank`, a loop counter that increments by exactly 1 on every row processed, rather than `row.scoreMs`, the real epoch-millisecond timestamp already available on each post.
Because `rank` only reflects the order rows came back from `this.posts.find({ order: { scoreMs: "ASC" } })`, the ZSET ends up sorted by seed/insertion order rather than by true chronological recency.

A post that is genuinely newer (larger real scoreMs) but happens to be seeded earlier in the loop receives a smaller rank value than an older post seeded later, so it sinks below that older post when the feed is read back.

getCachedFeed itself is correct: zrevrange(key, 0, 19, "WITHSCORES") reading the 20 highest-score members in descending order is exactly the intended read pattern for this cache; the defect is confined entirely to the write side in seedTimeline.

The fix is a one-line change — replace `rank` with `row.scoreMs` in the zadd call — so that a larger score corresponds to a later epoch timestamp, and the already-correct ZREVRANGE read then produces strict recency order.

Correctness after the fix should be verified by seeding posts in a shuffled, non-chronological order and asserting the returned timeline is strictly descending by real scoreMs/createdAt; two posts sharing the exact same scoreMs fall back to lexicographic ordering on postId inside the skip list, a separate edge case worth noting but not the bug itself.

Concatenating `pushedTimeline` and `celebrityPosts` without deduplicating by `id` breaks the moment an author is promoted from regular to KOL: both queries filter on the author's *current* celebrity flag rather than the flag at the time each post was written, so an author's older posts still sit in the push path while the same posts are now also pulled into the celebrity path, and every one of them renders twice in the merged feed.

The correct fix is a dedup pass keyed on `post.id` — for example building a `Map<string, Post>` or a `Set<string>` of seen ids while iterating the merged array and keeping only the first occurrence — applied right before the sort, not a change to either source query, since each query is individually correct and it is only the union that is wrong.

Because `this.getSaltedKolKey('kol_1', userId)` always passes the literal string `'kol_1'` instead of the celebrity's real `authorId`, every celebrity's cache is written and read under the exact same key family regardless of how many distinct KOLs exist in `celebrityIds`; once there is more than one celebrity, one celebrity's cache read can silently return another celebrity's cached timeline.

The fix for the salted-key bug is to pass the actual celebrity `authorId` being cached into `getSaltedKolKey` instead of a fixture id, and if the intent is one cache entry per KOL rather than one blended cache per reading user, cache each celebrity's timeline separately under its own real `authorId` and merge the cached results at read time instead of blending first and caching once under a shared identity.

Both the missing dedup and the hardcoded salted key are correctness bugs — the user is shown a wrong or cross-contaminated feed, not just a slow one — so they belong ahead of any cosmetic or stylistic PR comments and should be raised as blockers rather than nitpicks.

The tests passing and the demo timeline looking right prove nothing about the promotion case, since a single-snapshot dataset where no author's celebrity flag has ever changed can never exercise the stale-row overlap that causes the duplicate; the review has to explicitly reason about what happens the day an author crosses the threshold, not just about the code's current behavior.

A related but independent gap worth flagging is that nothing TTLs or deletes an author's stale push-timeline rows once they are promoted to celebrity, so even after the dedup fix lands, the duplicate-post problem keeps compounding on every future read unless a cleanup job or expiry handles the role-drift cleanup.

Concrete verification for these bugs means seeding an author as a regular user with existing posts, promoting them to celebrity, calling the hybrid feed, and asserting every `post.id` appears exactly once in the timeline; and separately seeding two distinct celebrities and asserting `getSaltedKolKey` resolves to two different keys rather than one shared key.

Setting `s-maxage=31536000` with `immutable` tells shared caches to hold a response for a year and tells clients the URL will never return different content — a promise that only holds when a URL is permanently bound to one piece of content, such as a content-addressed or versioned asset key.

A live playlist's payload mutates in place under the same key, so applying the static-asset directive to it means the edge caches the first response and keeps serving that same stale segment list to every viewer at that PoP for up to a year, with no natural mechanism to pick up the update.

The correct caching strategy for frequently-changing dynamic content is a short edge TTL such as `s-maxage=10` combined with `stale-while-revalidate`, which keeps the cache close to live state while absorbing revalidation cost without blocking clients.

Long-TTL `immutable` caching belongs exclusively to static, versioned assets whose URL changes whenever the underlying content changes — never to a key whose payload can change while the URL itself stays fixed.

When a handler throws an exception such as `NotFoundException` instead of returning an explicit response, the resulting error status carries no `Cache-Control` header of its own, leaving a shared cache free to apply its own default caching policy to that response.

Caching an unknown-key 404 turns a transient miss — a key not yet propagated from an upload pipeline, or momentarily absent mid-migration — into a sticky failure, since every viewer routed through that cache during the caching window keeps seeing 'not found' long after the origin would correctly serve the content.

The origin should answer unknown keys with a non-throwing 200-style fallback carrying an explicit short-TTL or `no-store` Cache-Control, giving the edge a deliberate, bounded instruction rather than leaving the outcome to a shared cache's default handling of an uncontrolled error status.

Locking this class of bug down in tests requires asserting the exact `Cache-Control` string per asset type — not just header presence — plus a separate test confirming an unknown key returns a bounded, non-cached response rather than being cached as a hard error.

`ensureTranscoded` guards against re-running the encode with a single check — whether `manifest.m3u8` already exists on disk — and nothing else; there is no lock or claim placed on a `videoId` before the ladder starts.

Because the existence check and the encode work are not atomic, every concurrent request for the same cold video (a `POST encode` call and several first `manifest.m3u8` fetches arriving together) sees the file missing at the same instant and independently starts the full three-rung FFmpeg ladder, multiplying CPU by the number of simultaneous requests instead of costing one ladder per video.

With no in-flight lock, these parallel ladders also race to write the same output files (segments and the master playlist), so whichever run finishes last wins and the others' encoding work is wasted or can corrupt the result.

The fix is coalescing concurrent callers onto a single run rather than adding a bigger lock around the whole method: keep an in-flight `Map<string, Promise<void>>` on the service, and once the existence check misses, look the `videoId` up in that map before starting any work.

If a promise for that `videoId` is already in the map, the caller awaits it and returns instead of starting a second run; if not, the caller starts the encode, stores its promise in the map synchronously before the first `await` so a concurrent caller sees it immediately, and removes the entry in a `finally` once the run settles.
This coalescing pattern is the same shape as request-deduping or dataloader batching, just keyed by `videoId` — it turns N concurrent first-requests for a cold video into exactly one FFmpeg run.

An in-memory map only protects a single process; if encoding must be durable across multiple server instances, `ensureTranscoded` needs to move onto a job queue (e.g. BullMQ) keyed by `videoId`, so a second instance also awaits the existing job instead of starting its own.

Lazy transcoding is the right default for a library where most uploads are never watched, since it avoids spending CPU on clips nobody opens, but it forces the first viewer of any video to wait out the full ladder before their manifest resolves.
Eager pre-encoding on upload makes the first play instant because the ladder already ran, but it burns CPU and storage transcoding effectively all uploads, most of which are never watched.

A reasonable middle ground is to eager-encode only content with an existing signal of being hot (an established creator, a flagged launch) and keep the lock-protected lazy path as the fallback for the long tail of uploads.

The metric that proves the coalescing fix worked is the count of concurrent FFmpeg processes, or `ensureTranscoded` calls that actually reach the encode loop rather than hitting the map and awaiting, per cold `videoId` — this scales with request concurrency before the fix and is pinned at exactly 1 after it.

A test that fires many concurrent `POST encode` calls for one fresh video id and asserts exactly one FFmpeg run occurred, producing one clean (non-corrupted) manifest, demonstrates the fix rather than just plausibly describing it.

When a proxy cache key is built from the full request URI, marketing query parameters like utm_source and utm_campaign become part of the key, so every share link to the same asset produces a distinct cache entry for identical bytes — this is cache pollution, and it prevents requests that should HIT from ever coalescing.

A Vary: Cookie header applied to every response, including public and non-personalized assets, makes the cache store one entry per session cookie instead of one shared entry per URI — an unbounded explosion that has nothing to do with the actual response bytes.

Vary: Accept-Encoding is only safe when it reflects a small canonical set of encodings (e.g. gzip, br, identity); varying on the raw, unnormalized Accept-Encoding header value fragments the cache into more entries than the number of distinct response bodies actually requires.

The fix for query-string pollution is to normalize the cache key: strip parameters that don't affect the response body (such as utm_* tracking params) and canonicalize the order of whatever parameters remain, so equivalent requests collapse onto the same entry.

Middleware that blanket-sets Vary: Cookie for session-aware responses must be scoped to only the routes whose output genuinely differs per user; it must never run in front of public, session-independent routes such as a CDN content/:key endpoint.

A falling HIT ratio paired with rising origin load points to a mismatch between the cache-key/Vary configuration and what actually changes the response, not to cache size or network/TLS problems — that mismatch is what forces otherwise-identical requests to MISS and fall through to origin.

Confirming a cache-key and Vary fix means watching the HIT ratio and the X-Cache-Status distribution climb back toward their pre-regression levels, and adding an alert on the HIT ratio so a future key or Vary regression is caught by the metric instead of discovered through an origin-load incident.

CORS is a browser-only enforcement layer checked by the client after the network response arrives, not a server-side constraint — a tool like curl that makes a raw HTTP request without a same-origin policy will show a clean 200 with correct bytes on a URL that a browser blocks entirely, because curl simply never performs the origin check that a browser does.

When a curl request against a URL succeeds while the same URL fails only in a browser, that asymmetry itself is diagnostic: it rules out the encoding pipeline, the file bytes, the status code, and the content-type as the cause, and narrows the fault to something the browser layer enforces on top of an otherwise-correct HTTP response.

The manifest handler explicitly sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` before calling `res.sendFile`, which is why the master playlist loads without issue in hls.js — the header is present exactly where it's needed for that request.

The segment handler never sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on either of its response branches — not the variant `.m3u8` playlist branch and not the `.ts` byte-serving branch — even though both branches correctly set `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control`.

A browser player using `fetch()` for segment requests is a cross-origin request whenever the player's page and the streaming service are served from different origins, a very common topology when content is fronted by a CDN; without a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, the browser blocks the response body from reaching the player's JavaScript even though the network layer received a valid HTTP 200 with the correct `video/mp2t` bytes.

The fix is to add `res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')` inside the segment handler for both branches (variant playlist and `.ts` segment bytes), because every HLS-serving endpoint needs the CORS header individually — setting it only on the manifest route is not sufficient for playback to continue past the first segment.

Verifying the fix requires reloading the page in an actual browser and confirming hls.js continues fetching subsequent segments with no CORS error in the console, or explicitly asserting that the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header is present on a segment response — re-running curl proves nothing, since curl never reproduced the failure in the first place and would show the same misleadingly-successful result before and after the fix.
A PURGE request that resolves without throwing only proves the HTTP call completed — it says nothing about whether the edge actually matched a stored entry and evicted it.

NGINX here keys its cache on `proxy_cache_key "$request_uri"` alone, but it still honors `Vary: Accept-Encoding` from the origin, so a single URI can back several cached variants split by content encoding.

The purge call goes out through an HTTP client shared with the service's other outbound requests, so it inherits that client's default `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` header even though a PURGE has no business carrying it.

Sending a PURGE with an `Accept-Encoding` header makes NGINX try to match one specific encoded variant; when that doesn't line up with what's actually cached, it's a Vary mismatch and NGINX answers 412 instead of evicting anything.

A non-error HTTP status is not proof of eviction: the handler builds `{ purged: true, key }` from the fact that the outbound request resolved, without ever inspecting the status NGINX actually returned.

The origin only delegates invalidation by firing the PURGE verb — the edge is the party that decides whether an entry is actually removed, so origin-side code that assumes success is trusting a system it doesn't control.

A durable fix needs two independent pieces: stop sending `Accept-Encoding` on the PURGE call specifically (a request-scoped header override or a dedicated client instance), and set `proxy_ignore_headers Vary` on the edge so it stores exactly one entry per URI regardless of encoding.

The only trustworthy way to confirm a purge worked is to issue a fresh GET through the edge right after and check that `X-Cache-Status` flips to MISS, rather than trusting the purge handler's own optimistic response body.

Moving the fs.unlinkSync cleanup calls to the end of the try block, right after the upload succeeds, means they only run on the happy path — the moment spawnFfmpeg or uploadFromFile throws, control jumps straight to the catch, which only marks the job FAILED and never touches the temp files.

Under that refactor, every encoder or upload failure leaves both temp files — the downloaded source tmpInput and the encoder output tmpOutput — permanently orphaned on disk, since the catch path never reaches the unlink calls.

This leak compounds with volume rather than being a one-off: on a box handling any real rate of failing transcodes, accumulating orphaned temp files trends straight toward ENOSPC, at which point even healthy jobs start failing because there is no disk space left to write to.

A finally block (or a deferred cleanup registered immediately after tmpInput/tmpOutput are computed, before anything that can throw) guarantees the unlink calls execute on every exit path, success and failure alike — that guarantee is the entire reason finally exists.

outputPath is derived purely from job.inputPath, with its extension swapped for a fixed -transcoded.mp4 suffix, and carries no per-job namespace — so retrying a FAILED job against the same inputPath computes the exact same key as the earlier attempt.

Because the key is unnamespaced, a retry silently overwrites whatever the previous attempt already uploaded to MinIO; the fix is to fold the job's own id into the key (e.g. `${job.id}/${base}-transcoded.mp4`) so every attempt writes to an isolated location.

The two defects differ in blast radius and should be reported in that order: the temp-file leak can degrade the entire host over time and eventually fail every job on it, while the key collision only corrupts the single job being retried.

Confirming both fixes calls for a failure-injection test — force spawnFfmpeg or uploadFromFile to throw and assert both temp files are gone afterward, and assert that two runs against the same inputPath never produce the same outputPath.

Splitting a queue-admit operation into a separate read (`ZRANGE`) and a separate delete (`ZREM`) means the read and the removal are two independent round trips to Redis, not one atomic step — anything can happen to the sorted set in between.

When two `admit()` calls run concurrently, both can execute their `ZRANGE` against the same front-N slice before either one's `ZREM` has taken effect, so both calls observe and remove the identical set of tokens — a classic read-then-remove race condition.

That race produces a double-admit: the same shopper token gets `SADD`-ed into the admitted set by two separate calls, which means one shopper is granted entry into two concurrent checkout sessions, cascading into oversell or double-charging further down the pipeline.

Replacing the `ZRANGE` + `ZREM` pair with a single `ZPOPMIN(key, count)` call collapses the read-and-remove into one atomic Redis command — since Redis executes commands single-threaded, no two concurrent callers can ever pop the same lowest-score members.

If the admit logic needs to grow beyond a plain pop — for example checking inventory or another condition before granting a slot — that extra logic has to be wrapped in a Lua script (`EVAL`) so the whole check-and-pop sequence still executes as one atomic unit on the server, rather than reintroducing a multi-round-trip race.

The admitted-tokens `SET` is never given an `EXPIRE`, so a shopper who is admitted but then abandons the flow (closes the tab, loses connection) leaves their token sitting in that set permanently, which means effective system capacity shrinks over time even while the waiting queue still has people in it.

Fixing the capacity leak means calling `EXPIRE` on the admitted key right after the `SADD`, with the TTL sized to the real p99 checkout completion time, so abandoned grants age out and their slots recycle back to the pool automatically.

Between the two defects, the double-admit race is the higher-severity issue because it breaks correctness and can directly cause oversell or duplicate charges, while the missing TTL is a slower, gradual degradation of capacity — a fix should be validated by firing concurrent `admit()` calls and asserting the returned token arrays are strictly disjoint, plus checking that the admitted key reports a positive TTL immediately after admission.

A pessimistic row lock acquired via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (or `lock: { mode: "pessimistic_write" }`) is held for the entire duration of the transaction, so any slow work placed after the lock is acquired — an external pricing API call, a remote audit-log write, extra SELECTs — is not paid once but is paid by every concurrent writer queued behind that same SKU row.

On a hot SKU during a flash-sale spike this turns into a serialization bottleneck: ten writers stacked behind one slow transaction means the tenth waiter's latency is roughly ten times the critical section's duration, which is exactly what pushes lock waits into statement or transaction timeouts.

The critical section should be shrunk to only the operations that actually need the row lock to stay correct: acquire the lock, check `stock >= quantity`, subtract the quantity, insert the ledger row, and commit — nothing else belongs between lock acquisition and commit.

The pricing API call never reads or writes the `inv` row it is locking, so it has no correctness dependency on the transaction and can be moved to run before the transaction opens (or dropped entirely if the result isn't actually used to decide anything).

The audit-log write is a call to a third-party service with no transactional relationship to the inventory row, so it should fire after commit rather than before — this way a slow or flaky audit service can never extend how long the row lock is held.

The extra `OrderEntity` and `PromoEntity` SELECTs are read-only lookups unrelated to the decrement decision, so they should either be computed outside the transaction or removed if they were never load-bearing for the write.

Even after trimming the transaction to its minimum, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` still serializes all writers on a single row, which is adequate at moderate volume but is the wrong mechanism to absorb the peak concurrency of a flash-sale spike itself.

Offloading the hot path to an atomic in-memory counter (a Lua script doing GET, compare, and DECRBY in one EVAL) removes the database from the critical path during the burst, and the counter can be reconciled back to the durable, lock-protected `inventories` row asynchronously via a queued job or scheduled sync, with a statement/lock timeout on the DB path kept as a backstop.

The fix should be validated by measuring p99 latency and the lock-wait/timeout rate under a concurrent burst on a single SKU before and after both trimming the transaction and offloading to the atomic counter, confirming throughput rises and timeouts drop while `inventories.stock` remains correct and non-negative.

Calling `zrange(QUEUE_KEY, 0, -1)` to compute a position forces Redis to walk its entire skip list, enumerate every member, and serialize the full N-length reply before any client-side work happens - this is an O(N) operation regardless of where the target token sits in the queue.

After the full member list arrives over the wire, `indexOf(token)` performs a second O(N) linear scan on the application side, so a single position lookup pays two separate O(N) costs stacked on top of each other.

A sorted set already maintains its ordering through a skip list, so `ZRANK` can walk directly to a member's position in O(log N) and return a single integer, with no transferring or scanning of the rest of the set.

Replacing `zrange` plus `indexOf` with `zrank` eliminates both the Redis-side enumeration/serialization cost and the client-side scan cost, not just one of the two, because the entire member list never has to leave Redis in the first place.

In a waiting-room system where every visitor polls every few seconds, the true cost of an O(N) endpoint comes from concurrent polling volume, not from any expensive business logic - a million waiters each triggering a full-set fetch is what saturates Redis CPU and network bandwidth at the same time.

Checking an admitted-visitors SET with `SISMEMBER` (O(1)) before ever touching the queue lets already-admitted visitors short-circuit immediately, avoiding even an O(log N) rank lookup for requests that do not need one.

Reducing how often a million clients poll - by backing off the interval or returning a server-computed estimated wait - cuts aggregate load in a way that a faster per-call algorithm alone cannot, since it addresses the request volume rather than the per-request cost.

A complexity fix should be confirmed with a load test at realistic scale, roughly a million queue members under concurrent polling, comparing p99 latency and Redis CPU/network utilization before and after, rather than assumed correct because the new code reads cleaner.

Wrapping a read-modify-write sequence inside `dataSource.transaction` only guarantees that the transaction's own writes commit or roll back together as a unit — it says nothing about whether another transaction can read or modify the same row while the first is still in flight.

Under the default Read Committed isolation level, `manager.findOne` without a lock option is a plain snapshot read, so two concurrent transactions can each fetch the same `stock` value before either one has written its result back.

When both transactions subtract `quantity` from that same stale in-memory value and then call `manager.save`, the second write simply overwrites the first without any awareness of it — a classic lost update — so the combined amount decremented can exceed the real stock and the system oversells.

Adding `lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' }` to the `findOne` call makes TypeORM emit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on that SKU's row, which forces a second transaction's read of the same row to block until the first transaction commits or rolls back.

Once the second transaction is forced to wait, its eventual read reflects the already-decremented stock rather than a stale snapshot, which serializes every decrement against that SKU and removes the lost-update window entirely.

Atomicity (a transaction's writes committing or rolling back as one unit) and serialized access to a row (mutual exclusion between concurrent transactions touching the same data) are two separate guarantees — a transaction boundary alone provides the former but not the latter.

The locked section of code should stay as small as possible — lock, check quantity, subtract, insert the ledger row, then commit — because holding a row-level lock longer than necessary increases contention and slows down concurrent requests during a flash sale.

Firing a burst of concurrent decrement calls against a small seeded stock, such as 200 concurrent decrement-by-1 calls against a starting stock of 100, is a concrete way to validate the fix: exactly 100 calls should succeed, the remainder should fail with an insufficient-stock error, and the final stock should floor at zero without ever going negative.

A check-then-set idempotency guard that runs `redis.get` followed by a separate `redis.set` leaves a gap between the read and the write; under two concurrent requests with the same key, both calls can read `null` before either has written anything, so both pass the `if (!existing)` check and both proceed to create an order.

Splitting the guard into two round trips reopens exactly the race the idempotency key exists to close — the key was meant to make "check ownership" and "claim ownership" a single event, and turning that into two separate Redis commands recreates a window a second caller can step through, the same shape as a `SELECT` then `INSERT` race, just one layer over on Redis instead of Postgres.

Collapsing the guard into one atomic command — `SET key PENDING EX 30 NX` — fixes the race because `NX` ("set only if the key does not already exist") makes the check-and-write a single un-interruptible Redis operation, so among any number of concurrent callers exactly one `SET` returns `"OK"` and every other caller immediately gets `null`, with no gap left for two callers to both slip through.

A caller that loses the `SET NX` race should not retry the write blindly; it must issue a follow-up `GET` on the key and branch on the value — if the value is still `PENDING`, the original request is still in flight and the caller should respond with a conflict (409, retry later); if the value is a cached result, the original request already finished and the caller should return that result marked as a replay instead of creating a new order.

Even with an atomic Redis claim, the database layer still needs its own safety net: a `UNIQUE` constraint on the idempotency key column catches the case where a second write still slips past Redis, for example a `PENDING` key's TTL expiring mid-flight or a Redis flush/restart wiping the claim before the original request finished.

When the unique constraint fires, the insert throws a database error (for Postgres, a `QueryFailedError` carrying error code `23505`) rather than silently succeeding, so the calling code must catch that specific error, re-read the already-created row by the idempotency key, and return it as a replay instead of letting a raw 500 reach the client.

Correctness of the fix should be demonstrated with two concurrent requests sharing the same idempotency key: exactly one call ends up creating the order while the other is rejected or receives a replayed result, and the orders table ends up holding exactly one row for that key.

Replaying a cached idempotency result without comparing it against the incoming request body means a client that reuses the same idempotency key with a different payload — for example a changed order amount — silently receives the old, now-incorrect response instead of an error.

The correct fix for key reuse with a changed body is to store a fingerprint (a hash such as SHA-256 of the request payload) alongside the cached result at write time, then recompute and compare that fingerprint on every replay lookup: a match replays safely, a mismatch must return 422 Unprocessable Entity rather than replaying stale data or silently processing the new request as if it were unrelated.

Wrapping the Redis lock-acquisition call in a try/catch that returns an 'ACQUIRED' state on any error is a fail-open design: once Redis becomes unreachable, every concurrent request is treated as if it won the lock, so the idempotency guard stops preventing duplicates for the entire outage window rather than degrading gracefully.

Fail-closed is the correct posture for an idempotency guard: when the underlying lock store is unavailable, the operation should reject or surface a 503 Service Unavailable instead of proceeding as if the guard succeeded, because letting every request through defeats the purpose of having a guard at all.

A database UNIQUE constraint on the idempotency key is a valid last-resort safety net, but only if the application catches the resulting unique-violation error; leaving it uncaught means a legitimate concurrent retry crashes with a raw, unhandled 500 instead of receiving the successful result of the request that already completed.

Handling a caught unique-violation correctly means re-fetching the already-persisted row by its idempotency key and returning it as a replay response, mirroring the same replay behavior used on the fast Redis-cache path so that both the cache route and the database-constraint route converge on identical client-facing behavior.

Layered idempotency protection works as defense-in-depth: the cache (e.g. Redis) optimizes the common case for speed, the database unique constraint is the durable invariant that holds even when the cache is down or racing, and the body fingerprint is what distinguishes a legitimate retry of the same operation from a different operation that mistakenly reused the same key.

When reviewing a change like this, the highest-severity issues to flag first are the ones with the largest blast radius — silent data corruption from an unvalidated replay and a guard that stops guarding under failure — ahead of lower-impact concerns like unhandled exceptions surfacing as generic errors, and the review should include concrete test cases: same key with a changed body returns 422, the store being down still yields exactly one persisted record via the database constraint, and a retry racing an in-flight write replays instead of failing with a 500.
An `INCR` on a per-cell demand key with no TTL or expiry does not measure live pressure — it accumulates into a running total since the key was first created, so the number only ever goes up.

Once a cell's demand pushes the multiplier past `SURGE_CAP`, `Math.min(raw, SURGE_CAP)` keeps returning the cap for the rest of the day even after real demand has dropped back to zero, because nothing ever decrements or resets the counter.

The practical effect is that riders in a cell that was busy earlier (e.g. lunch rush) get charged the day's cumulative peak price hours later, at 3am, with no live demand at all — this is an overcharge driven by stale data, not current conditions.

Making demand decay fixes the root cause: setting a TTL on the key right after incrementing it (or writing with `SET ... NX EX` so a live key isn't reset early) causes idle cells to cool back down on their own.

A more accurate alternative to a single TTL'd counter is a real sliding window — a sorted set of request timestamps trimmed with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` — so demand reflects only recent activity rather than a single decaying value.

`const supply = SUPPLY_BASELINE` is a second, independent defect: a hard-coded constant has no relationship to how many drivers are actually free in a given cell, and does not move when a driver goes offline, gets locked by another rider, or comes back online.

Supply should instead come from a live signal — such as a bounded geo-search over active drivers (e.g. `GEOSEARCH` on a drivers geo-index) or a maintained per-cell available-driver counter updated as drivers connect, lock, and release.

The demand-decay bug is the higher-priority issue to flag in review because it directly overcharges riders for pressure that has already passed — a trust problem — while the static supply baseline is a real but secondary accuracy improvement.

A regression test for the fix should drive a cell's quotes up until the multiplier hits the cap, stop generating demand, advance the clock past the TTL or window, and then assert that the next quote's multiplier has fallen back toward 1.0.

Running GEOSEARCH with BYRADIUS and no COUNT forces Redis to walk every geohash cell touching the full radius before any distance pruning happens, so a 50km circle hands back a candidate set far larger than anything a rider match actually needs.

Capping the radius to a business-appropriate constant and adding a COUNT parameter lets Redis stop early once it has the nearest handful of sorted candidates, shrinking both the geohash cell walk and the size of the downstream candidate list.

Awaiting `redis.exists` inside a for-loop, once per candidate, is a textbook N+1 pattern: each check is its own network round-trip, so end-to-end latency grows linearly with the candidate count even though the EXISTS lookup itself is sub-millisecond work on Redis's side.

Collapsing the per-driver EXISTS calls into a single ioredis pipeline turns many sequential round-trips into exactly one, which matters more for tail latency under load than shrinking the GEO query itself, since the N+1 loop is the dominant cost.

A periodic sweeper — a cron job or a keyspace-notification listener that runs ZREM on drivers whose heartbeat has expired — keeps the GEO key itself mostly clean over time, so the per-query online filter has progressively less stale data left to check.

Reducing round-trips does not by itself prove the optimization is safe: validating it requires asserting the returned driver set is identical before and after the change for a normal-size radius, while separately confirming the round-trip count drops and p99 latency measurably improves.

The exact radius cap and COUNT value are a business tuning decision rather than a fixed technical constant — setting them too small risks under-returning drivers in sparse areas, so the numbers need to be chosen and validated against real matching needs per market.

If the sweeper falls behind on removing expired heartbeats, stale entries can still pass the per-query EXISTS filter, letting the online/offline signal drift out of sync with the GEO key between sweeper runs.

A Redis key, no matter how many shards the cluster has, is pinned to exactly one shard by hash slot - so when every rider near a stadium maps to the same H3 cell, both the `demand:<cell>` counter and the `drivers:geo` GEO key become single hot keys that funnel thousands of operations per second onto one shard while the rest of the cluster idles.

The bottleneck here is per-key operation rate, not total data volume: the number of drivers around the stadium is modest, but the INCR and GEOSEARCH calls against those two keys arrive far faster than a single key on a single shard can absorb.

Raising the H3 resolution around detected hot spots, or sub-partitioning the demand counter into several sub-keys (for example keyed by a hash of `riderId`) and summing them back on read with `mget`, spreads the same total demand across multiple keys instead of concentrating it on one.
Sharding `drivers:geo` by region (for example `drivers:geo:<regionId>`) keeps one busy area's traffic from sharing a shard with the geo index for the entire city.

Batching near-simultaneous match requests into a single `GEOSEARCH` per tick (using `pipeline()` for the round-trips) and serving `supply` from a short-lived snapshot with a 1-2s TTL cuts the number of live reads against the hot keys instead of hitting them once per rider.

Each mitigation carries a real cost: finer or more cells mean more empty cells to skip and a wider k-ring before a driver is found, batching adds a small queueing delay before a rider sees a quote, and a snapshot cache trades read relief for a bit of staleness in the reported supply figure.

Validating the fix means replaying the stadium's traffic pattern in a single-cell load test against both the original and the modified version, comparing per-key QPS and p99 latency on that one shard, and confirming nearest-driver accuracy and surge correctness have not regressed.
Redis's GEOADD command follows the mathematical (x, y) axis convention, expecting arguments in the order key, longitude, latitude, member — latitude comes second, not first.

Swapping latitude and longitude still produces a syntactically and semantically valid pair of numbers for GEOADD, so Redis accepts and stores the coordinate without any validation error; it just encodes a location on the opposite side of the (lng, lat) convention, for example landing Ho Chi Minh City's (10.76, 106.66) somewhere off the coast of West Africa.

An always-empty nearby-driver result combined with drivers actively pinging and zero thrown exceptions is a signature that data was written to the wrong place, not that the query logic itself is broken — this points investigation toward the write path (GEOADD) rather than the read path (GEOSEARCH).

Both the write (GEOADD) and the read (GEOSEARCH with FROMLONLAT/BYRADIUS) execute successfully as syntactically valid Redis commands even with the coordinates swapped, which is exactly why this class of bug throws no exception anywhere and can ship unnoticed — only the underlying data is wrong, not the code path.

A one-line reorder of the arguments fixes the immediate symptom, but the durable fix is structural: funnel every position write through a single method that takes an explicitly named `{ lat, lng }` parameter and performs the swap into `(lng, lat)` internally in exactly one place, so no caller can pass raw positional coordinates directly into a GEO write.

A proving regression test writes a driver at a known coordinate, then runs the nearby search with a very small radius (e.g. 10m) around that exact point and asserts the driver comes back at roughly zero distance — this test fails against the swapped-argument version and passes once the order is corrected.

Because GEO writes and reads are two separate operations with no cross-validation, an argument-order bug in the write path is invisible to any error handling on the read path, making it a class of bug that silently corrupts data while every individual operation reports success.

A check-then-set pattern that reads a lock key and then writes it as two separate Redis round-trips leaves a window in which a second concurrent caller can read the same "no lock" state before the first caller's write lands, so both callers proceed as if the resource were free.

In this matching flow, two ride requests resolving to the same nearest driver can both execute `redis.get(lockKey)` and see no lock before either executes `redis.set(lockKey, '1')`, so both fall through the guard, both remove the driver from the geo set, and the driver ends up assigned to two riders at once.

This is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race: the vulnerability lives in the gap between the check operation and the use (write) operation, not in Redis itself — individual Redis commands are atomic, but two separate commands issued back-to-back are not atomic as a pair.

Replacing the GET-then-SET pair with a single `SET key value NX` command makes lock acquisition atomic: Redis guarantees that of several concurrent NX writes racing on the same key, exactly one succeeds and returns OK while the rest return null, eliminating the interleaving window entirely.

Because the atomic SET NX resolves the race deterministically, only the request that wins the lock should remove the driver from the matching pool; a request that loses the lock must fall through and try the next candidate driver in the ring rather than treating the failed lock as an error.

Giving the lock key an expiry (EX) is a separate concern from atomicity: even with SET NX, a process that errors or crashes after winning the lock but before confirming the trip would otherwise leave the driver permanently locked and unmatchable, so a TTL bounds how long a driver can be stuck by an abandoned lock.

Ordering the operations correctly — acquire the atomic lock first, then remove the driver from the pool — ensures a driver is only pulled out of circulation once a lock has actually been won, so a request that loses the lock never removes a driver it doesn't own.

This class of bug is invisible to sequential, single-request tests because the failure only manifests under true concurrency; verifying a fix requires firing multiple simultaneous requests at the same driver and asserting exactly one succeeds while the rest fall through or fail, ideally also confirming the unfixed check-then-set version fails that same test as a negative control.

Constructing a new Redis client with `new Redis(...)` inside every request handler opens a fresh TCP connection and performs a full Redis handshake on every single call, instead of reusing one connection across requests.

At high request volume — thousands of location pings per second — that per-call connection cost exhausts the process's available file descriptors or Redis's own `maxclients` ceiling long before the service becomes CPU-bound.

The correct pattern is a single shared `ioredis` client built once behind a DI provider (bound to a token such as `REDIS_CLIENT`) and injected into the service's constructor, so one durable connection is reused and pipelines commands for the entire app lifetime.

A Redis sorted set used for `GEOADD` has no concept of per-member expiry, so a driver's coordinate remains in the `drivers:geo` key indefinitely once written, even after that driver goes offline or the process crashes mid-shift.

Without a cleanup mechanism the GEO key only grows over time, turning into a big key and becoming a source of ghost matches — nearby-driver results that still include drivers who are no longer actually online.

Filtering stale drivers at query time, such as checking a heartbeat key with `EXISTS`, hides ghost entries from the API response but does not shrink the underlying sorted set, so a periodic sweeper job is still needed to actively `ZREM` expired members and keep the key's size bounded.

A test suite that exercises only a single driver doing one write and one read at low load cannot expose either defect, because connection exhaustion and unbounded key growth only manifest once concurrency or driver churn crosses a volume the tests never approach, so a green suite proves nothing about production readiness.

Proving the fix actually works requires a soak test under sustained load with drivers cycling online and offline, asserting that both the process's open-connection count and the GEO key's member count stay flat over time instead of climbing.

A document in this BM25 index is represented in two places at once: the record itself in `docs`, and scattered traces of it across the posting list of every term it once contained in `postings`. Deleting only from `docs` leaves the second representation completely untouched.

When a deleted document's id is left inside a term's posting list, that document can still be pulled into the scoring loop the next time the term is queried — `termFrequency` resolves to 0 once `docs.get(id)` is undefined, so the entry scores 0, but the id can still surface in the returned result set.

IDF's document-frequency count `n` is computed from the size of a term's posting list, so leaving a deleted document's id inside every posting list it belonged to keeps `n` artificially inflated — this understates IDF for that term for every OTHER still-valid document, not just the deleted one.

A term whose only owning document gets deleted becomes orphaned: its posting list is never emptied and the term key is never removed from `postings`, so `vocabSize` never shrinks even though the live corpus has actually gotten smaller.

Decrementing `N` without also subtracting the deleted document's length from `totalLength`/`docLengths` makes `avgdl` (totalLength / N) drift upward, which skews the BM25 length-normalization term for every remaining document on every subsequent query — not just ones touching the deleted document's terms.

This kind of bug is insidious because nothing throws and `search` keeps returning results that look plausible; the corruption is a silent, gradual degradation of ranking quality rather than an immediate, visible failure.

A correct delete must read the document's `content` and re-tokenize it BEFORE removing it from `docs`, since that is the only place the content still exists — this recovers exactly which terms the document contributed so each one's posting list can be cleaned up.

For each recovered term, a correct delete removes the document's id from that term's posting list, and if the list becomes empty as a result, removes the term key from `postings` entirely — only after posting-list cleanup and length-stat updates are complete should `docs.delete(id)` and the `N` decrement happen, since all of postings, docLengths, totalLength, and N must move together.

Correctness can be proven with a concrete test: index two documents sharing one term plus a third document that owns a term uniquely, delete the document with the unique term, then assert that term is gone from `postings`, `vocabSize` dropped by exactly one, and the remaining documents' scores shift to reflect the freshly recomputed IDF and avgdl.

Serializing the entire in-memory index to a single JSON blob on every mutation makes write cost proportional to the total index size rather than to the size of the change — adding one token still walks every term's posting list and every document record, so cost is O(index size) per write instead of O(delta size).

This pattern is write amplification: as the corpus grows, each small addDocument or removeDocument call pays the full-corpus serialization cost, so both CPU spent in JSON.stringify and bytes written to Redis scale with corpus size rather than with how much actually changed, causing throughput to collapse under high-ingest load even though individual writes are tiny.

The fix is to stop rewriting the whole snapshot on every mutation and instead persist only the delta — appending an operation-log entry (or a small immutable segment) per mutation — and reserve the full compacted snapshot write for a slower background schedule, so a write's cost becomes proportional to the mutation rather than to the whole index.

One incremental approach is an append-only log: push just `{ op, id, content? }` onto a Redis stream on each mutation (cheap, O(1) per write), then periodically or once the log passes a size threshold, run a full serialize-and-set to compact it; on boot, load the last full snapshot and replay the log entries after it to reconstruct an identical index.

An alternative is the Lucene segment model, where each batch of mutations becomes a new small immutable JSON segment, a background job periodically merges old segments together, and boot reads every live segment to rebuild the index.

Incremental or segment-based persistence trades away simplicity for performance: it introduces compaction/merge logic and crash-recovery bookkeeping (e.g., handling a process dying mid-append or mid-segment-write) and tombstone handling for updates/deletes, whereas the single full-snapshot write is simpler and always internally consistent — a reasonable choice for a single-node, low-ingest, or teaching-scale service.

The choice between full-snapshot and incremental persistence should be driven by ingest rate and corpus size, not treated as a correctness bug versus a solution — full-snapshot writes are a deliberate simplification whose acceptability shrinks as ingest rate and corpus size grow.

Verifying the fix requires benchmarking write latency and CPU against corpus size before (expected linear growth) and after the change (expected flat/constant cost), plus a restart or rebuild test asserting the reconstructed index is identical to the one that existed before restart.

When two upstream calls are independent — the second call's input doesn't depend on the first call's output — awaiting them sequentially (`await fetchRanked(bm25); await fetchRanked(vector)`) makes total latency the sum of both engines' latencies instead of the max, even though nothing in the business logic required that ordering.

Firing the two upstream calls concurrently with `Promise.all([fetchRanked(bm25Url, ...), fetchRanked(vectorUrl, ...)])` collapses total latency from bm25Latency + vectorLatency down to roughly max(bm25Latency, vectorLatency), since both calls are now in flight at the same time.

`Promise.all` alone does not bound the tail: it still resolves only once every promise in the array settles, so a single hung engine still pins the whole request — just with a lower floor than before, since the other branch is no longer adding on top of it.

Bounding the tail requires a timeout on each upstream call individually, not just on the aggregate: wrapping each `fetchRanked` call in an `AbortController`, calling `controller.abort()` from a `setTimeout`, and passing `{ signal: controller.signal }` into `fetch` causes that specific call to reject with an `AbortError` once its own budget expires.

A timed-out call should degrade to an empty result list — for example via `.catch(() => [])` on that branch — rather than letting the `AbortError` propagate and fail the whole request; this reuses the same failure-isolation path already used for a genuinely dead upstream, so RRF fuses whatever results did come back.
Because BM25 and vector search are independent engines with no ordering dependency between them, running their calls in parallel is safe and introduces no new race condition or correctness risk.

The `limit * 2` over-fetch is a separate, orthogonal concern from latency — it exists to protect ranking quality (making sure a consensus document survives fusion) and doesn't need to change as part of a latency fix.

Correctness of the fix should be verified two ways: confirming p99 drops to roughly max(bm25Latency, vectorLatency) after parallelizing, and injecting an artificially slow or non-resolving engine to confirm the request still returns within the timeout window with partial results instead of hanging.

On the index path, `tokenize()` normalizes text by lowercasing it and splitting on runs of non-alphanumeric characters, so a document containing "Redis" ends up stored under the key `redis` in `this.postings`.

`queryTokenize()` was added later, lives only inside the query handler, and does not reuse `tokenize()` — it merely splits on whitespace and keeps the original case, so the same word can produce a different token depending on which of the two paths processed it.

Because the query token `Redis` and the indexed key `redis` differ only in case, `this.postings.get(term)` returns undefined for a document that genuinely contains the word — the index path and query path have silently drifted out of sync with each other.

A Map lookup miss is not an error condition in JavaScript/TypeScript, it simply returns undefined, so the `if (!posting) continue` guard skips the term without throwing or logging anything, which makes an empty or partial result look like a legitimate "no match" rather than exposing the bug.

Two independent tokenization implementations that are supposed to agree but are edited separately have no crash-shaped failure signature, so an empty result set with zero exceptions is itself the diagnostic clue pointing at a normalization mismatch between index-time and query-time processing, not a BM25 scoring defect.

The correct fix is to delete `queryTokenize()` entirely and call the same `tokenize()` function from `search()`, guaranteeing the index path and query path always normalize text identically and can never diverge again.

After the fix, re-running the query `Redis` (different case than the stored `redis`) should return the previously missing document, and a regression test asserting that index-time and query-time tokenization produce identical tokens for the same input guards against a future edit to only one of the two paths reintroducing the bug.

This failure mode generalizes beyond casing: any asymmetric normalization step applied on only one of the two paths — a stemmer, a stopword filter, synonym expansion — produces the same silent, exception-free recall collapse, so the durable fix is a single shared normalization pipeline rather than a patch for the specific case difference.

"No error, plausible-looking similarity scores, but degraded ranking" is the signature of an embedding-space mismatch rather than a runtime bug - there is no exception or log to chase because cosine similarity always returns a valid float no matter which model produced the vectors.

Each embedding model learns its own coordinate space during training, so a vector produced by one model and a vector produced by a different model do not live in the same space, even when both happen to output the same dimensionality.

Cosine similarity computed between a query vector from one model's space and document vectors from another model's space still executes and returns an arithmetically valid number in a normal-looking range - that number simply carries no semantic meaning.

In this code, EmbeddingService (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) still embeds documents through the nightly reindex job, while this deploy wired SearchService to QueryEmbeddingService (all-MiniLM-L12-v2) for queries, so two different models feed vectors into the same column.

A dimensionality mismatch, meaning different vector lengths, would throw right at insert or comparison time against a fixed-size pgvector column; this bug stays silent specifically because both models happen to output exactly 384 dimensions, so no data-layer check catches the discrepancy.

The fix is to point search() back at the same embedding service used for indexing and remove the extra QueryEmbeddingService dependency entirely, so the index path and query path can never again be wired to two different models by mistake.

If the real goal is to finish migrating to the newer model rather than roll back, the entire documents table must be re-embedded under that model before both paths are pointed at it - a table can never be left holding vectors from two different models at once.

Validating the fix requires more than eyeballing a query: running a known paraphrase pair against its expected ranking confirms the model mismatch was really the cause, and measuring recall on a labelled sample after re-embedding confirms quality actually recovered.

BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus-dependent — they shift with term rarity, document length, and index size — while cosine similarity is naturally bounded to [-1, 1], so the two lists don't measure the same kind of quantity to begin with.

Min-max normalizing each list separately to [0, 1] only rescales each list onto the same axis labels; it doesn't make the underlying quantities comparable, so summing the two normalized values produces a number with no real relevance meaning.

A single outlier score in one engine's list — one document scoring far above the rest — stretches that list's min-max range and squashes every other document's normalized value toward zero, letting the outlier dominate the fused sum almost regardless of what the other engine reports.

Because min-max normalization is relative to whatever scores happen to be in the current result set, a shift in one engine's score distribution — reindexing, a corpus change, a scoring tweak — changes a document's normalized value and therefore the fused ranking, even though the document's actual rank and relevance haven't moved at all.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps both failures by fusing on each engine's integer rank rather than its raw score, summing 1/(k+rank) with k = 60 — rank is always comparable across engines no matter what a raw score means or how its distribution shifts, so there's no normalization step left to be fragile.

A constructive code review affirms that combining both engines' signal into one ranking is the right goal, and frames rank-based fusion as the standard, battle-tested way to reach that goal rather than treating the author's intent as wrong.

Regression tests for a score-fusion function should specifically cover an outlier-score scenario and a distribution-shift scenario, asserting that a rank-based fusion keeps the ranking stable in both cases where the min-max version would visibly break.

Each reject branch in a compensating cascade must DECR exactly the set of tiers that were already INCRed above it in that same run — here the tenant-reject branch never DECRs the user key it INCRed, and the global-reject branch DECRs only the tenant key while leaving the user key permanently inflated.

Because bump() increments the user tier before the tenant and global verdicts are known, a reject at either later tier leaves the earlier tiers' counters holding an increment that was never actually granted unless it is explicitly rolled back before returning.

The fix is mechanical: add redis.call('DECR', KEYS[1]) on the tenant-reject branch, and add the same DECR on the user key alongside the existing tenant DECR on the global-reject branch, so every reject path fully undoes everything incremented before it.

This increment-then-conditionally-reject pattern behaves like a small saga — each rollback must undo every prior step's effect, not just the immediately preceding one, whenever a later step in the cascade fails.

The leak produces no error and no crash because every individual redis.call the script issues (GET, INCR, PEXPIRE, the one DECR it does call) succeeds on its own terms; the bug is a missing call rather than a failing one, so there is no exception path or log line to surface it.

The visible symptom is gradual over-throttling rather than an outage: userCount and, on a global reject, tenantCount silently drift upward relative to the number of requests actually granted, so identical traffic gets throttled more tightly over time with no error to point to.

Keeping the whole increment-check-rollback sequence inside one EVALSHA/Lua script call keeps the compensation atomic, so no other request evaluated through the same cluster.evalsha call can ever observe the user or tenant counters in their briefly over-incremented state.

Correctness of the fix is proven by driving traffic that rejects at each tier in turn — user, tenant, global — and asserting afterward that userCount, tenantCount, and globalCount each equal exactly the number of requests actually granted at or below that tier, with zero residual drift.

Sending the full Lua script body via EVAL on every consume call re-transmits roughly a kilobyte of text per request, and Redis must hash (and recompile, if it isn't already the cached script) that body before running it — a cost that scales linearly with RPS instead of staying flat.

This is a transport/bandwidth problem, not a correctness problem: the Lua script already executes atomically on Redis's single thread, and that guarantee is unaffected by how the script text reaches the server.
Calling SCRIPT LOAD once — for example in onModuleInit — registers the script body with Redis and returns a 40-character SHA1 digest that can be cached on the service instance for reuse.

Replacing eval(LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET, ...) with evalsha(sha, ...) sends only the short digest per request instead of the full script body, cutting per-call payload from roughly a kilobyte down to about 40 bytes.

The refill-then-deduct logic inside the Lua script itself does not change at all — only the wire format of how the client invokes it changes, so the algorithm and its atomicity are identical before and after the optimization.

Switching to EVALSHA introduces a new failure mode: if Redis restarts or a SCRIPT FLUSH runs, the server no longer has the script cached, and calling evalsha with the old SHA throws a NOSCRIPT error even though the client still holds a valid-looking digest.

A NOSCRIPT error needs to be caught and handled by reloading the script (SCRIPT LOAD again, or a one-off EVAL fallback for that single request) and retrying with the freshly reloaded SHA, so a single cache flush never takes the rate limiter down.

The improvement should be confirmed with a before/after load test: correctness stays intact (a concurrency=20 run against capacity=5 still yields allowedActual: 5), while p99 latency and CPU per request should visibly drop once only the digest travels per call instead of the full script text.

A sliding-window log limiter that stores one ZSET member per in-window request keeps memory usage proportional to request volume, so a client sustaining ~10k requests per minute ends up with ~10k entries live in Redis for that key alone.

Each admission check on that log pays `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` (evict expired entries) plus `ZCARD` (count survivors), an O(log N + M) cost — and because N grows with traffic, the busiest keys are exactly the ones paying the highest per-check cost, which is the wrong direction for a hot path.
A weighted two-bucket counter replaces the per-request log with just two integers per client, `curr` and `prev`, one for the current window-sized bucket and one for the previous.

The sliding count is estimated as `prev * (1 - elapsedRatio) + curr`, fading the previous bucket's contribution smoothly as the current bucket fills rather than resetting sharply at a window boundary; this turns both memory and per-operation work into O(1), independent of request volume.

This estimator is an approximation, not an exact count — it trades a small, known error (on the order of 0.003% at reasonable traffic) for eliminating the O(N) memory blow-up and the eviction/count cost on hot keys.

Because the counter is approximate, any use case where the count itself is the source of truth — billing, contractual/hard quotas, audit trails — needs to stay on the exact ZSET log; only clients that are both genuinely hot and tolerant of a small margin of error should be migrated to the counter.

Rolling out a new counting mechanism as a drop-in replacement for an exact one carries a correctness risk that can't be resolved by inspection alone — it needs to be validated against the structure it's replacing under realistic load before being trusted for real traffic.

That validation takes the form of running both implementations side by side — driving the same requests through the exact log and the new counter and comparing their outputs — and confirming the counter's estimate stays within the accepted error bound at the target request rate before any hot client is actually cut over to it.

In a Redis ZSET, the member is the unique identity of an entry while the score only determines its sort order for range operations — two `ZADD` calls with the same member do not create two entries, the second call simply overwrites the score of the existing one.

The given code calls `ZADD key now now`, using the millisecond timestamp `now` as both the score and the member, so any two requests that compute the same `Date.now()` value collide on the exact same member.

Because `Date.now()` only has millisecond resolution, a burst of concurrent requests can easily produce identical timestamps, making same-member collisions realistic under load rather than a rare edge case.

When a same-millisecond collision happens, the second `ZADD` overwrites the first entry instead of adding a new one, so only one member ends up stored in the ZSET for two requests that were actually granted.

The subsequent `ZCARD` call then reports one fewer entry than the number of requests truly admitted, so the limiter compares an undercounted value against `limit` and keeps granting requests past the configured threshold.

The fix is to keep the score as `now` — so `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` window eviction still works correctly by time — while making the member unique per request, for example `${now}-${randomUUID()}` passed as the ZADD member argument.
Separating the ordering key (score) from the identity key (member) lets concurrent same-millisecond requests each occupy their own ZSET entry without breaking the time-based eviction logic.

Correctness can be verified by firing many requests concurrently within a single millisecond (e.g. `Promise.all` over `limit + 5` calls) and asserting that `ZCARD` equals the number of calls that returned `allowed: true`, with the `(limit + 1)`th request correctly denied.
Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16384 hash slots and, by default, computes a key's slot as `CRC16(key) mod 16384` over the entire key string.

Three unrelated key names such as `quota:u:<userId>`, `quota:t:<tenantId>`, and `quota:g` share no common substring, so they almost certainly hash to different slots and can even be owned by different nodes.

A Lua script executed via `EVALSHA`/`EVAL` is only allowed to touch keys that all resolve to the same slot, because Redis needs that guarantee to run the script atomically and single-threaded on one node without cross-node coordination.

When keys span multiple slots, Redis Cluster rejects the command outright with `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`, which is exactly why the endpoint 500s on every call once deployed to a cluster.

Standalone Redis has no concept of hash slots — every key lives on the same single node — so a multi-key script over `quota:u:*`, `quota:t:*`, and `quota:g` works there by accident, not because the key naming is correct.

A hash-tag fixes this by wrapping the substring the keys should share — here the tenant id — in curly braces, e.g. `` `{q:${tenantId}}:u:${userId}` ``, `` `{q:${tenantId}}:t` ``, `` `{q:${tenantId}}:g` ``.

Redis Cluster's slot-hashing rule has a special case: when a key contains a `{...}` substring, only the text inside the first pair of braces is hashed, so all three keys sharing the same braced tag land on the same slot and node and the multi-key script becomes atomic again.

Forcing all of a tenant's keys onto a single slot via a shared hash-tag concentrates that tenant's entire quota traffic onto one node, so a very large tenant can turn that node into a hot spot; the standard mitigation is to sub-shard the tag (e.g. append a bucket to the tag) for such tenants, at the cost that cross-bucket state for that tenant is no longer atomic in a single script.

Calling `ZADD` unconditionally, before the `count < limit` check even runs, means the sorted set records every request that hits the key — accepted and rejected alike — instead of only the ones that actually consume quota.

When a client is flooded far past its limit, that unconditional `ZADD` keeps writing one new member per attempt into the ZSET regardless of the reject decision, so the set's memory footprint scales with total attempts rather than with the configured `limit`.
The count check itself is correct — it does gate the allow/reject decision properly — the bug is purely in the bookkeeping that happens one line earlier and independently of that decision.

The fix is to move `ZADD` inside the branch where `count < limit`, so the sorted set only gains a member when a request is actually granted, and to return early on the reject path without touching the ZSET at all.

Restructuring around a 'record-on-grant' rule bounds the ZSET to roughly `limit` entries per active client, since denied requests never get written, no matter how many times an abusive client retries.

The key also has no `PEXPIRE`, so a legitimate client that sends a few requests and then goes silent leaves its ZSET sitting in Redis forever — nothing ever reclaims it because `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` only trims on the next call to that key, which never comes.
Calling `PEXPIRE(key, window)` right after every successful `ZADD` makes an idle key self-expire after one window of inactivity, closing the second, independent leak from the record-on-reject bug.

Verifying the fix means flooding one key with far more requests than its limit and asserting the ZSET's cardinality stabilizes near `limit` instead of climbing with the attempt count, then confirming the key's TTL expires it once traffic stops.

A shared cache keyed only on `$request_uri` cannot distinguish between different logged-in users hitting the same path, so a personalized response stored under that key gets replayed to every later requester regardless of who they are.

Sending `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` on a per-user endpoint like `/me` tells any shared cache in front of the origin that the body is safe to store and reuse across clients, even though the body actually differs per session — that turns a caching config into a cross-user data leak, not just wasted cache capacity.

Responses that carry authentication state — a request with an `Authorization` header or `Cookie`, or a response with `Set-Cookie` — must bypass a shared/edge cache entirely; only genuinely public, unauthenticated GET responses belong in that cache.

Fixing the leak requires two coordinated changes: the handler must mark `/me` `private, no-store` (or omit `Cache-Control`, which defaults to non-cacheable), and the edge must add `proxy_cache_bypass`/`proxy_no_cache` keyed on `$http_cookie`/`$http_authorization` so authenticated requests never read from or write into the shared cache.

`proxy_cache_valid any 1h` applies the same hour-long TTL to every status code the origin returns, including 4xx and 5xx, so a single transient `500` gets pinned in cache and replayed to clients for an hour after the origin has already recovered.

Error responses should be given a much shorter negative-cache TTL than success responses, or excluded from caching altogether — caching a transient failure for as long as a valid success response turns a momentary origin blip into an extended, self-inflicted outage.

With `proxy_cache_lock off`, every request that arrives after a hot cache entry's TTL expires misses at the same instant and is forwarded to the origin concurrently, producing a stampede; turning `proxy_cache_lock on` makes nginx admit exactly one of those requests to refill the entry while the rest wait for it.

Proving the fix works takes concrete before/after evidence, not just a config read-through: requesting the personalized endpoint as two different authenticated users must return different bodies with no leakage between them, and forcing then repairing an origin error must show the edge stop serving the stale error once the shorter negative TTL has elapsed.

A synchronous SELECT to read the current offset followed by an UPDATE to persist the new one against the Postgres `upload_session` row runs on every single chunk PATCH, so on a multi-GB upload split into thousands of 1MB chunks, that pair of round-trips is multiplied thousands of times and dominates PATCH latency far more than the SHA256 hashing or the dedup lookup.

The offset is validated and advanced on every chunk, but it only needs to be durably persisted occasionally rather than on every write — treating every check as a durability event is what turns a cheap operation into a database bottleneck.

Splitting the offset into two tiers — a fast Redis key such as `upload:<sessionId>` for the live value and Postgres for the durable record — lets each PATCH validate and advance the offset with an O(1) Redis GET/SET instead of a Postgres findOneOrFail followed by an update.
Postgres still owns the durable `upload_session` row, but it is written for status and recovery purposes rather than being the thing every chunk's validation blocks on.

Redis in this design is a rebuildable hot cache, not a second source of truth: if the key evicts or Redis restarts mid-upload, the offset can be reconstructed from the committed chunk total already durable in Postgres and the Redis key reseeded before the next PATCH is served.

A cold or missing Redis cache costs only one extra reconstruction read against Postgres — it never corrupts or silently loses the tracked offset, because Postgres remains the authoritative record throughout.

This is the classic speed-in-the-hot-tier, durability-in-the-cold-tier trade-off: Redis buys low-latency validation on the hot path while Postgres continues to guarantee the upload can never lose or misplace its true progress.

Verifying the fix requires two checks: measuring PATCH latency before and after the split to confirm it drops from two Postgres round-trips to roughly one Redis round-trip plus an occasional durable write, and deliberately killing Redis mid-upload to confirm the offset rebuilds correctly from Postgres so the upload resumes at the exact right byte.

A fixed TTL with no jitter means every concurrent reader of the same hot key shares an identical expiry moment, so the instant that boundary passes, all of them see a cache MISS at the same instant rather than staggered over time.

This synchronized MISS is a cache stampede (thundering herd): each of the ~50k concurrent readers independently falls through the edge cache straight to the shielded origin at the same instant, instead of one request rebuilding the entry on behalf of the rest.

`proxy_cache_valid 200 60s` only governs when a cached entry goes stale — it says nothing about how many concurrent requests are allowed to react to that staleness by hitting the origin, so origin CPU/DB load spikes periodically in lockstep with the TTL rather than staying steady.

Request coalescing via `proxy_cache_lock on;` fixes the root cause by letting exactly one of the concurrent MISSes actually reach `/api/cdn/origin/:fileId/:chunkIndex` to rebuild the entry, while every other concurrent request for that same cache key waits on that single in-flight rebuild instead of independently calling the origin.

Pairing coalescing with `proxy_cache_use_stale updating;` lets the edge keep answering the other waiting requests with the still-cached, slightly stale chunk during the rebuild window, so those clients get an immediate 200 instead of blocking behind the lock until the single rebuild finishes.

The staleness this introduces is bounded to roughly one origin round trip — the time the single coalesced rebuild takes (the 150ms `readChunk` cost) — which is a deliberate, acceptable trade-off in exchange for turning tens of thousands of simultaneous origin hits into one.

Because the origin sets an `ETag` from the chunk's SHA256, the single coalesced rebuild request can revalidate as a cheap `304 Not Modified` instead of re-sending the full chunk body, making the one allowed-through request even cheaper than a full refetch.

The fix can be verified by driving concurrent load against the same fileId/chunkIndex exactly across a 60s expiry boundary: before the fix the origin sees a burst of roughly 50k hits at each expiry, and after adding `proxy_cache_lock` plus `proxy_cache_use_stale updating;` the origin sees roughly one request per key per refill cycle while `X-Cache` still shows a clean MISS-then-HIT/stale pattern with no error responses.

A PATCH writeChunk handler that takes a client-supplied `sha256` field and uses it directly as the chunk's identity — for both the dedup lookup and the derived storage object key — is trusting client-declared metadata as if it were a cryptographic fact, without ever recomputing the hash from the actual received bytes.

Content-addressable storage systems rely on the invariant that a key always equals the hash of the bytes it points to; skipping the recompute step and substituting a client-asserted value breaks that invariant at the exact point where untrusted input crosses into the storage layer.

If the claimed hash happens to collide with an existing `chunk_dedup` entry, the request is treated as a dedup HIT and returns the object key for that entry — silently serving back bytes that belong to different content than what the client actually uploaded.

If the claimed hash does not yet exist, the handler inserts a brand-new `chunk_dedup` row keyed by that unverified hash, creating an entry whose stored bytes no longer equal the hash of its own key — this is index poisoning, and every future lookup of that hash inherits the corruption.

Because the server never independently verifies the claim, the same bug also lets ordinary transit corruption go undetected: bytes that got mangled in flight are still filed under whatever hash the client originally declared, with no check that the two still agree.

The correct fix is to decode the request bytes first and then compute the SHA256 digest server-side from those exact bytes (e.g. `createHash("sha256").update(data).digest("hex")`), using only that recomputed digest — never the client-supplied value — as the identity for both the dedup lookup and `objectKeyFor(...)`.

The client's `claimedSha` should be downgraded from an identity input to a verification assertion: compare it against the server-recomputed hash, and reject the request with a 400 `sha256_mismatch` error before any lookup or write happens if the two disagree.
