This is a general trust-boundary principle, not a hashing-specific one: any identity, key, or address that a client can freely name for data it also supplies must be independently derived or verified server-side, exactly the same discipline applied to validating any other untrusted input.

`Buffer.alloc(CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES)` allocates a full 1MB buffer that Node zero-fills by default, and `Buffer.prototype.copy` only writes as many bytes as actually exist in the given source range — for every full chunk that source range holds a full 1MB, but for the file's final chunk the range runs past `payload.length`, so `copy` writes fewer real bytes and the remainder of the buffer stays at its original zero-fill.

Hashing `buf` instead of the real byte range means the digest for the final chunk is `sha256(real tail bytes + zero padding)`, not `sha256(real tail bytes)` — the padding silently becomes part of what gets content-addressed.

This breaks dedup identity: the same real tail bytes, stored elsewhere as their own complete object or as the true final chunk of another identical file, hash to the digest of just those bytes — a different, unpadded digest — so a lookup against this chunk's padded hash never matches.

It also breaks integrity verification: a check that reads back the actually-stored bytes and re-hashes them (correctly, unpadded) can never reproduce the recorded padded digest, so a file that is not actually corrupt gets flagged as corrupt.

`size: CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES` is hard-coded on every chunk regardless of how many bytes were really copied, so for any file whose length is not an exact multiple of the chunk size, `sum(chunk.size)` comes out larger than the file's true `totalSize` — the invariant that chunk sizes must sum to the file's total size is silently violated alongside the hash bug.
The fix keeps the fixed 1MB windowing scheme untouched and only removes the padding: hashing and sizing must operate on the real byte slice, not an allocated fixed-size window.

Using `payload.subarray(i * CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES, (i + 1) * CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES)` directly avoids the bug entirely, because `subarray` clamps its end to `payload.length` automatically — the final window comes back shorter with no manual `Buffer.alloc` or `copy` step, and hashing that slice plus recording `size: slice.length` makes the last chunk legitimately smaller than 1MB.

With the fix, chunks `0` through `N-2` are computed exactly as before (unaffected, since their source ranges were always full), while the last chunk's hash now represents only real bytes and `sum(chunk.size) === totalSize` holds again, restoring both dedup identity and the size invariant.

Storing the chunk manifest as a single JSONB array on the file row makes sha256 unindexable, since it lives inside array elements rather than as a real column — a global dedup lookup ("does this sha256 exist anywhere?") degrades into scanning and parsing every file's array instead of hitting an index.

The same structural limitation blocks the resumable-upload query "which chunkIndex is missing for this file?" — that answer can only be computed client-side after fetching and parsing the whole array, not expressed as a WHERE clause.

Updating a single chunk under this design requires reading the entire chunks array, mapping over every element to change one, and writing the whole array back in one UPDATE — an N-chunk file rewrites all N chunk entries to change just one, which is significant write amplification.

This read-mutate-write pattern is not concurrency-safe: two requests updating two different chunks of the same file each read the array before either writes back, so whichever update lands second silently overwrites the first request's change — a lost update with no error raised.

Keeping chunkCount as its own hand-maintained column alongside the chunks array creates a second fact about the same data with no single source of truth; nothing stops it from drifting away from the actual chunks.length if a future write path forgets to keep both in sync.

The fix is the normalized file (1) -> chunk (N) model: a ChunkEntity with a unique index on (fileId, chunkIndex) and an index on sha256, with chunkCount derived from COUNT(*) (or trusted only because the insert is transactional) rather than hand-carried.

A JSONB blob is genuinely simpler when the only operation is fetching the whole manifest and handing it to the client in one row read with no join — the trade-off only tips toward normalization once "does this chunk exist" or "which chunk is missing" become the steady-state queries.

The recommendation can be validated concretely: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a sha256 filter should show an Index Scan rather than a Seq Scan after normalizing, and firing two concurrent updates at two different chunks of the same file should show neither update lost.

Outlinks are the current state of a page, not an accumulating history — the set returned by `extractOutlinks()` on each parse represents exactly what the page links to right now, and any write path that only inserts treats the link table as an append-only log instead of a snapshot.

`this.linkRepo.save(records)` in `parse()` never deletes prior rows for the same `fromUrl`, so re-crawling a page only ever adds edges: parsing `a` when it links to `b` and `c` writes `a→b` and `a→c`, and if `a` is re-parsed later linking only to `c`, the stale `a→b` row is left sitting in `page_link` alongside the newly written `a→c` row.

Because PageRank computes `PR(u)` by summing contributions over `in(u)`, every stale inbound edge left behind by a shrinking outlink set inflates the in-degree — and therefore the PageRank — of the target URL, even though that URL is no longer actually linked to.

This bug produces no exception or error of any kind, so it drifts silently over months of re-crawls; the only observable symptom is that rankings on a real corpus gradually stop making sense, which makes it very hard to trace back to its source.

The correct replacement semantic is delete-then-insert: before saving the newly extracted records, delete every existing row where the source column equals the page being re-parsed (e.g. `this.linkRepo.delete({ fromUrl: url })`), then insert the fresh outlink set, so the table always converges to exactly the current outlinks rather than a superset of every set ever seen.

An upsert keyed on `(fromUrl, toUrl)` is not a substitute for the delete step — it correctly updates or inserts rows whose pair already appears in the new set, but it does nothing to a row whose pair is simply absent from the new set, since that pair was never part of the new batch being upserted at all.

A delete-then-insert write path is idempotent under re-parsing: running `parse()` any number of times against the same HTML always leaves `page_link` holding exactly the current outlink set for that page, never accumulating duplicates or leftovers from earlier parses.

The fix can be verified concretely by re-parsing the same page with a smaller outlink set than a previous parse and asserting that both `storedLinks` and the actual row count in `page_link` for that `fromUrl` equal the new, smaller count — not the cumulative total of every parse ever run on that page.
Storing the full HTML as a plain text column inline in the same row as url/host/statusCode means each row's size is dominated by the page body rather than the small metadata fields.
Once a text value exceeds roughly 2 KB, Postgres moves it out-of-line into TOAST storage, which bloats the table's physical footprint and skews the query planner's row-width statistics.

Because TOAST bloat and skewed statistics affect the whole table, metadata-only queries such as listing pages or looking up by host slow down even though they never select htmlBody, since they still scan a table whose rows are secretly huge.

Separating the heavy blob from the hot metadata fixes the root cause: push the raw HTML to object storage such as S3 or MinIO under a key derived from the page (e.g. a hash of the URL or a UUID), and keep only a content digest plus that object key in the page row alongside url/host/statusCode/contentType.
A content digest — a hash of the HTML body — doubles as a cheap way to detect duplicate or unchanged pages without re-reading the full HTML on every crawl.

With the blob moved out, the write path still upserts a small metadata row as before, but the body write goes through an object-storage put call instead of populating htmlBody, so a metadata scan now touches a table of small, fixed-width-ish rows with no TOAST involvement.

Inline text storage is not inherently wrong and is genuinely fine at demo or small scale; the trade-off only tips toward object storage at billions of rows, where the extra network hop to fetch the body when actually needed (rendering, re-parsing, re-indexing) and the added consistency burden between Postgres and the object store are worth paying to keep the frequently-queried metadata table small and fast.

The migration's benefit can be verified concretely by comparing metadata-query latency and table-plus-TOAST size before and after the change, and by confirming the HTML is still retrievable end-to-end through its stored object key.

The `enqueue` method issues `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` as three separate awaited Redis calls with no atomicity between them, so two workers enqueuing the same brand-new URL can both read the membership check as a miss before either has run `BF.ADD`, and both then push the URL onto the ZSET as a duplicate.

Each enqueue on this path pays three sequential network round trips to Redis (one for the existence check, one for the bloom add, one for the queue add), and because each awaited call must finish before the next starts, that round-trip count directly caps how many URLs the frontier can accept per second.

The check-and-set can be made atomic and single-round-trip by fusing `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` into one Lua script and registering it as a custom ioredis command (for example via `redis.defineCommand`), since Redis runs a Lua script as one atomic, single-threaded server-side operation.

Because the fused script runs as a single atomic unit, no second worker can observe the bloom filter mid-check, which closes the double-add race entirely, and replacing three awaited calls with one round trip raises enqueue throughput roughly 10x.

Bloom-filter dedup for a crawler is inherently best-effort, so an occasional double-enqueued brand-new URL is generally harmless — the Lua-script fuse is worth making specifically when exactly-once enqueue semantics are required or the system is throughput-bound on enqueue, not as a default change to every code path.

Correctness of the fix can be verified by concurrently calling enqueue with the same brand-new URL from many clients and asserting the queue's size grows by exactly one instead of accumulating duplicate entries.

The throughput claim can be verified by benchmarking enqueues-per-second on the original three-call sequential path versus the single fused Lua-script call, comparing the numbers before and after the change.

`this.redis.get(cacheKey)` has the return type `string | null`, where `null` signals a genuine cache miss (the key was never set, or its TTL expired) while an empty string `""` is a legitimate cached value.
An empty robots.txt body is a meaningful, valid result — it means "no restrictions apply" — so storing it in the cache as `""` is correct behavior, not an edge case that needs to be filtered out.

In JavaScript, empty strings are falsy, so a truthiness check like `if (cached)` cannot tell apart "nothing was cached" (`null`) from "an empty value was cached" (`""`) — both fall through to the same branch.

Because the cache-hit branch tests truthiness instead of `cached !== null`, a host whose robots.txt is empty makes every request fall into the else branch, refetch `/robots.txt`, and overwrite the cache with the same empty string, even though the previous write's 60-second TTL was still valid.

The TTL itself and the `redis.set` call both behave correctly; the defect is entirely on the read side — the cached value is never successfully recognized as a hit for these hosts, so it always looks like a miss.

Hosts whose robots.txt content is non-empty never trigger the bug, since any non-empty string is truthy, which is why the failure hides silently and only affects a specific subset of hosts rather than breaking the cache uniformly.

Replacing the truthiness check with an explicit presence check, `cached !== null`, fixes the bug by treating "a value was returned from Redis" as the cache-hit signal, regardless of whether that value happens to be an empty string.

The fix can be verified by seeding the same host's empty robots.txt twice within the 60-second TTL window and confirming `fakeFetch`/robots.txt fires only once, or by checking the Redis TTL on `crawler:robots:<host>:body` to confirm the key is being read rather than repeatedly overwritten.

The enqueue path never calls `BF.RESERVE` before issuing `BF.EXISTS`/`BF.ADD`, so RedisBloom auto-creates the `seen:urls` filter on the very first bloom command it sees, using its own built-in defaults rather than any values configured in the service.

RedisBloom's default sizing for an auto-created filter is roughly a 0.01 error rate and a capacity of exactly one hundred items — which is why the frontier stalls right around the hundred-URL mark rather than at some arbitrary point.

Once real inserts exceed a bloom filter's reserved capacity, its actual false-positive rate climbs well past the advertised rate, so `BF.EXISTS` starts reporting brand-new URLs as already seen and the crawler wrongly discards them as duplicates.

A bloom filter has exactly one failure mode — the false positive — and returning a false positive is normal, non-error behavior; nothing throws or logs, so the frontier silently stops accepting most URLs instead of surfacing an error.

The fix is to explicitly call `BF.RESERVE(key, errorRate, capacity)` with the real configured values on module init (or lazily before the first enqueue), sizing capacity to roughly 1.5x the expected number of unique URLs to leave headroom for growth.

`BF.RESERVE` throws if the target key already exists, so the reserve call must be wrapped in a try/catch that swallows only the "item exists" error — this makes the reserve idempotent across restarts, re-asserting the correct configuration without wiping out dedup state a previous instance already built.

The fix can be verified by checking `BF.INFO` to confirm the filter's reported capacity matches the configured value instead of the silent default of one hundred, then enqueuing well past a hundred distinct URLs and confirming none of them are rejected as false duplicates.
A dangling node in PageRank is one with out-degree zero — it has no outlinks at all, so under the bare recurrence its rank mass has nowhere to flow.

In this loop, the inner accumulation `for (const v of inLinks.get(u) ?? [])` only gathers rank FROM other nodes' inlinks; there is no separate step anywhere that collects a dangling node's rank and redistributes it back across the graph.

Because dangling mass is never redistributed, the sum of the `rank` map drifts below 1 after every pass of the `for (let it = 0; it < MAX_ITERATIONS; it++)` loop, and the resulting rank ordering becomes unstable across iterations.

The fix is to compute, each iteration before building `newRank`, a `danglingSum` equal to the sum of `rank.get(u)` over every node whose `outDegree` is zero, then derive `danglingShare = (DAMPING * danglingSum) / N` and add that share to every node alongside the existing `teleport = (1 - DAMPING) / N` term so the rank vector re-normalizes to sum to 1.

This bug is dangerous precisely because the code still runs to completion and returns superficially plausible numbers; the decay only becomes visible on a real corpus containing dead-end pages, which is why it slips past shallow or toy-graph tests.

In code review, the tell is structural rather than a runtime error: there is no variable resembling `danglingSum` or `danglingShare` anywhere near the main iteration loop, signaling the redistribution step was simply never written.

A regression test for this class of bug should assert that `[...rank.values()].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` stays approximately 1 after every single iteration, run against a graph that deliberately includes at least one dangling node so the faulty path is actually exercised.

The missing correction is conceptually the same kind of uniform redistribution as the teleport term — both `teleport` and `danglingShare` add a flat amount to every node per iteration, so omitting the dangling term is easy to overlook since the code superficially resembles a correct damped power-iteration implementation.

A lease acquired via `SET NX PX` plus a Lua CAS renew guarantees at most one *active* leader at any instant, but it does not guarantee that only one process ever executes leader-only code — a process can stop actively participating (for example during a GC pause) without immediately learning that its lease has expired.

A leader that pauses for longer than `leaseMs` can lose its lease to a newly elected successor while paused, then resume execution still holding `isLeader = true` in its own local memory, because nothing inside the process itself was notified that the lease had expired and a successor took over.

When the resumed, no-longer-actual leader goes on to execute a non-idempotent external write — such as charging a customer or sending a batch of emails — with no term or fencing value and no idempotency key attached, the same side effect can fire twice: once from the true current leader and once from the stale one.

Attaching a monotonic term (a fencing token) to the side effect, and having the downstream system such as a payment gateway reject any call whose term is lower than the last one it accepted for that resource, closes this hole because a stale leader's writes always carry an outdated term.

Alternatively, making the write idempotent — for example keying it by something like `${jobDate}:${customerId}` — lets a stale replay collapse into a no-op at the receiving system, so correctness no longer depends on the leader-election layer alone.

Setting `renewIntervalMs` equal to `leaseMs` leaves no safety margin: a single slow or missed renew call, such as one delayed Redis round-trip, lets the lease expire before it is renewed and triggers an unnecessary failover; the renew interval should instead be a fraction of the lease length, roughly a third or less, so several renew attempts fit inside one lease window.

In a design review, the unfenced non-idempotent side effect is the blocking issue — it can silently double-charge customers or duplicate emails — and it should be raised and prioritized separately from the renew-interval timing, which is a comparatively minor tuning nitpick.

Whether this design is actually safe under a paused-leader or false-failover scenario can only be confirmed by a test that deliberately forces a leader to pause across a term boundary and then asserts that the downstream system rejects or deduplicates the stale-term write instead of executing it a second time.

A default `etcd3` read is linearizable, meaning it triggers a ReadIndex confirmation: before answering, the leader verifies via a majority heartbeat that it is still leader. No log entry is written, but the client still pays roughly one leader round-trip per read.

Calling `.serializable()` on an `etcd3` `GetBuilder` skips the ReadIndex confirmation entirely and answers straight from whichever replica received the request. This is nearly free but can lag the true committed state by tens of milliseconds — a bounded staleness, not an unbounded one.

Reads split into two categories by what they're used for: reads that DECIDE something (who holds a lock, who is leader, critical config) versus reads that only DISPLAY something (a dashboard count, a metrics aggregate). This distinction, not raw call frequency, determines which consistency mode a read needs.

A stale answer on a lock-owner or leadership read can hand the same lock or leadership role to two different callers at once, so that read must stay linearizable — it cannot be switched to `.serializable()`.

A dashboard or metrics read that is off by tens of milliseconds causes no correctness problem, only a slightly stale display value, so it is safe to switch to `.serializable()` and read from the local replica instead of paying the round-trip on every poll.

The fix is a per-call routing decision, not a global consistency downgrade: only the reads that tolerate staleness get `.serializable()` added; reads that gate a decision are left on the default linearizable path untouched.

The win can be proven by measuring p99 latency under load for both paths — the switched-over dashboard read should drop close to a local read, while the lock-owner read stays at roughly one round-trip, unchanged.

The routing rule itself should be enforced by a test, not just documented: spy on the underlying `get(...).exec()` call for the lock-owner read and assert that `.serializable()` is never chained onto it, so a future edit can't silently weaken a decision-making read.

A hardcoded, single lock key such as "jobs" makes every worker contend for the exact same resource no matter which job it actually popped off the queue, so N independent workers doing unrelated work collapse to the throughput of one.

The lock key should encode the specific resource being protected, e.g. `jobs:${job.id}`, so workers processing different job ids acquire different keys and run fully in parallel — only a genuine same-job-id conflict, such as a retry racing the original attempt, still contends.

Even after sharding the key, every acquire attempt — including ones that end up refused — still pays the full cost of N parallel SET NX PX round-trips across all nodes plus the validity computation, so granularity fixes parallelism but does not remove per-attempt overhead.

Setting the per-node commandTimeout close to the TTL (e.g. 900ms against a 1000ms TTL) leaves almost no headroom: one slow node can consume nearly the entire TTL just acquiring the lock, pushing computed validity to zero or negative and forcing a wasted re-acquire.

A safe sizing rule keeps commandTimeout to roughly 10% or less of the TTL and keeps the actual critical section — the real work done while holding the lock — to roughly 30% or less of the validity window, rather than letting either crowd the full TTL.

If the protected work genuinely needs more time than that headroom allows, the correct fix is to raise the TTL itself, not to let commandTimeout or an oversized critical section eat into the remaining validity.

Neither lock sharding nor TTL/timeout resizing weakens correctness: acquisition still requires agreement from a quorum of independent nodes for liveness, and every write is still checked against a monotonic fencing token to reject a stale holder — only what is locked and for how long changes, never the safety guarantees.

The fix can be validated with a throughput test comparing the single global key against the sharded per-job-id keys under the same load, confirming throughput now scales with the number of distinct job ids in flight and that no two workers ever simultaneously hold the lock for the same job id under either scheme.

In the leader/renew branch, calling `pexpire` on the lease key every tick without first confirming the key's stored value still matches this node's own id extends whatever lease currently occupies that key, regardless of which replica actually owns it.
A replica's local `isLeader` boolean is never re-verified against Redis during renew, so once the underlying key changes ownership the flag can go stale and stop reflecting reality.

If a network blip or slow tick makes a node miss its renewal window, its lease expires and a follower's `SET leader_key myId PX <ttl> NX` legitimately claims the key — yet the demoted node's next tick still calls `pexpire` on that same key, extending a TTL that now belongs to the new leader.
The result is split brain: two replicas both hold `isLeader === true` at the same time and both execute the leader-only job concurrently, even though only one of them actually owns the Redis key.

This failure mode never surfaces under a single-leader smoke test or normal operation, because on the happy path renew always lands before expiry and the key's value never changes underneath the current leader — it only appears after an actual lease-expiry event such as a blip or GC pause.

The correct renew operation is an atomic compare-and-swap executed server-side, e.g. a Lua script that runs `GET` on the key, compares it against this node's own id, and only calls `PEXPIRE` when they match, returning a sentinel value (such as 0) on mismatch.

Redis executes Lua scripts single-threaded, so folding the ownership check and the TTL extension into one script closes the race window that exists when `GET` and `PEXPIRE` are issued as two separate client round-trips.

When the compare-and-swap script reports a mismatch, the node must immediately set `isLeader = false` and log its step-down instead of retrying the renew, falling back to competing for the key via `SET ... NX` like any other follower.

A distributed lock's usable window is not the raw `ttlMs` passed in — it is `ttl − elapsed − drift`, where `elapsed` is however long the acquisition itself took and `drift` compensates for clock skew between the independent Redis nodes voting on the lock.

Because `Promise.all` over the per-node `SET NX PX` calls has no per-node timeout, a single slow or dead node can stretch the real acquisition time close to the full `ttlMs` before the quorum resolves — so `elapsed` can end up nearly as large as `ttl` itself.

Hard-coding `validityMs: ttlMs` in the return value — instead of computing it from `Date.now()` captured before the parallel `SET` calls and subtracted afterward — means the reported validity is completely disconnected from how much of that window the acquisition itself already consumed.

The grant condition should be `acquiredOn >= quorum && validityMs > 0`, not just `acquiredOn >= quorum`; when the computed validity is zero or negative the function must fail closed — releasing the lock on every node and returning `acquired: false` — exactly like the existing failure branch already does for a missed quorum.

The bug is silent on the happy path because when all nodes are healthy, `Promise.all` resolves almost instantly, so real elapsed time is tiny and even a correct calculation would land close to `ttlMs` — meaning the missing `elapsed`/`drift` subtraction never visibly changes the result under normal conditions.

With `ttl=5000ms` and one node taking roughly 4800ms to respond, the real remaining validity is only about 200ms minus drift, yet the unfixed function still reports `validityMs: 5000` and `acquired: true` — so a worker believes it holds the lock for nearly five more seconds when it is already almost expired, letting a second worker acquire the same resource and both believe they hold a valid lock simultaneously (the exact split-brain scenario Redlock's quorum mechanism exists to prevent).

Fixing the acquisition path alone is not sufficient — the `ioredis` client should also have `commandTimeout` (and `connectTimeout`) configured to well under roughly 10% of `ttlMs`, so a single dead node is bounded and cannot drag the whole `Promise.all` call out toward the full `ttl` the way it does in the unbounded version.

Even after correctly computing `validityMs`, the critical section protected by the lock should still finish comfortably inside that window — typical guidance is using no more than about 30% of it — since a shrunk validity is not license to consume every remaining millisecond, leaving margin for release and any residual jitter.

etcd assigns a Raft-ordered `createRevision` to a key at the moment it is written, and that value is already returned in the PUT response header (`putRes.header.revision`) rather than needing to be computed by the client.

Stamping a queue position with `Date.now()` on the client makes ordering depend on wall-clock time, and clocks on different machines can drift, so concurrent joins can leave two clients each believing they hold the head position.
`modRevision` (etcd3's `kv.mod_revision`) changes every time a key's value is written, while `createRevision` is fixed at the moment the key is first created and never changes afterward.

Sorting a queue by `modRevision` instead of `createRevision` causes the queue order to silently reshuffle whenever any ticket's value is updated, even though the ticket's actual join order never changed.

etcd supports server-side ordered retrieval — `getAll().prefix(prefix).sort("Create", "Ascend")` — which returns entries already sorted by creation order and removes the need for the client to compute or re-sort ordering itself.

A single-client demo has no concurrency and no mid-queue updates, so both the wall-clock-position bug and the modRevision-sort bug pass local testing while still being production-breaking under real concurrent load.

Client-computed ordering undermines the core reason to build a queue on etcd in the first place: etcd's Raft consensus already provides a total order across writes, so recomputing that order client-side reintroduces the exact race the system exists to remove.

A correct implementation keeps ticket ordering pinned to `createRevision` even when a ticket's value later changes, such as a progress field being updated mid-queue, since `createRevision` is immutable while `modRevision` moves with every subsequent write to that key.

Writing balance updates directly with `UPDATE account SET balance = $1 WHERE id = $2` and no corresponding `ledger_entry` row bypasses the ledger entirely, breaking the double-entry invariant `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)`.

Once the ledger and the cached `account.balance` diverge this way, the invariant check exposed at `GET /api/invariant` starts reporting a mismatch that has nothing to do with an underlying bug — the reconciliation "fix" itself is what caused it.

Without a `ledger_entry`, nothing distinguishes an automated system correction from a customer genuinely moving that money, so replaying the event log makes the correction look as if it never happened.
Without a `reconciliation_run` row, there is no way to answer when reconciliation last ran, what drift it found, or what it fixed — the audit history a proper reconcile loop is expected to persist.

The correct fix is a compensating `ledger_entry` shaped like a real transfer: the delta computed as a `BigInt`, direction set to `DEBIT` or `CREDIT` depending on sign, and a `compensating: TRUE` flag marking it as an automated correction rather than customer activity.
The compensating ledger entry insert and the `account.balance` update must happen together inside a single transaction (`BEGIN`/`COMMIT`), never as a bare `UPDATE` issued outside of any ledger write.
A `reconciliation_run` row should be inserted alongside the fix, capturing the trigger, the drift count, and the fixes applied, so each correction is traceable to a specific run.

The fix can be verified by calling `GET /api/invariant` and confirming `balanced: true`, and by querying `ledger_entry WHERE compensating = TRUE` to see the correction appear as a flagged, run-linked row rather than an untraceable balance edit.

The invariant endpoint runs two full-table `SUM(amount)` aggregations — one for DEBIT, one for CREDIT — over the entire `ledger_entry` table on every call, so its cost is O(rows) and grows without bound as the ledger grows.

`ledger_entry` is append-only and immutable: rows written yesterday never change, so re-summing the whole table from scratch on every 30-second poll re-derives an answer that was already correct before, wasting work on settled history instead of just accounting for new rows.

The correct fix is turning the aggregate from something RECOMPUTED on read into something MAINTAINED on write — a `ledger_summary` table (or a Postgres materialized view) that holds the running `totalDebits`/`totalCredits` and is updated the moment a transfer happens, rather than a blind cache slapped in front of the existing query.

The running totals can be updated inline, inside the exact same `BEGIN…COMMIT` transaction that already inserts the debit/credit `ledger_entry` rows, so the summary can never drift out of sync with what was actually written — or updated asynchronously through a CDC stream, such as Debezium tailing the Postgres WAL, feeding a small consumer that applies each new row to the summary.

If a materialized view is used instead of a hand-maintained summary table, it needs a periodic job — for example a NestJS `@Cron()` task — to run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` so the view stays reasonably current.

After the fix, `GET /invariant` becomes a single-row read like `SELECT totalDebits, totalCredits FROM ledger_summary`, which is O(1) regardless of whether `ledger_entry` holds thousands or billions of rows.

`account.balance` is already an example of this exact write-through-cache pattern, updated inline with every transfer, which is why per-account balance reads are already O(1); only the global invariant check was still doing the expensive full recompute.

Moving to an incrementally maintained total introduces a new risk — a bug in the increment logic or CDC consumer could silently drift from the truth — so a periodic authoritative full-table SUM, such as a nightly reconciliation job, must still run and alert loudly the moment it diverges from the cached totals, keeping the cheap O(1) check honest without paying its cost on every poll.

A nightly full scan that walks every account regardless of recent activity is bound by two independent constraints at once — the total account count and a single concurrency=1 worker draining the queue serially — so once the account base reaches billions, no amount of per-query speedup removes that ceiling; the bottleneck is architectural, not a slow SUM query.

Partitioning the account base (by id hash, by country, or by product line) into separate queues, each with its own worker, turns one serial walk over the entire dataset into many partitions reconciling in parallel, directly addressing the throughput ceiling.

An activity-driven filter — a CDC stream off the ledger table (e.g. Debezium), or a lighter mechanism like Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY — lets a run skip accounts with no new activity since the last cut-off, instead of recomputing the ledger SUM for every account whether or not it changed since yesterday.

Partitioning and activity-driven filtering solve two different kinds of waste and are complementary rather than substitutes for each other: partitioning alone still re-sums every untouched account inside each partition, while filtering alone still funnels every matching account through a single worker per partition.

Keeping each partition's queue at concurrency=1 preserves the original safety property that no two workers can ever race on the same account and post two separate compensating entries for the same drift.

Reconciling against a single cut-off timestamp captured once at the start of a run, rather than an open-ended 'now', prevents a transaction still in flight from the external truth source from being mistaken for drift.

Introducing a CDC-driven path adds a new risk that the original full scan didn't have: a dropped or missed change event would silently hide real drift, so running a periodic full, unfiltered sweep alongside the activity-driven path (e.g. weekly) acts as a backstop that proves the filtered runs aren't missing anything.

Taking row locks in the order arguments happen to arrive in a request — first `fromAccountId`, then `toAccountId` — instead of a deterministic order makes the lock acquisition sequence depend on transfer direction, which is the actual root cause of an intermittent Postgres `deadlock detected` error, not anything wrong with the SQL itself.

When a transfer A→B and a concurrent transfer B→A both run `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the same two accounts in opposite orders, the A→B transaction locks A and then blocks waiting for B, while the B→A transaction locks B and then blocks waiting for A — each transaction ends up holding exactly the row the other one needs next, forming a classic ABBA cycle.

Postgres's deadlock detector recognizes this wait-for cycle and resolves it by aborting one of the two transactions with a `deadlock detected` error while letting the other proceed, which is why the failure surfaces as an intermittent 500 rather than a hang.

Single-direction transfers on a given account pair never trigger this deadlock because only one transaction is touching the pair at a time — the cycle only forms when two transactions traveling in opposite directions race on the same pair of accounts concurrently.

The fix is to make lock acquisition order independent of transfer direction by sorting the two account ids and always locking the smaller one first, ideally in a single query such as `SELECT ... FROM account WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` with the id array pre-sorted.

Once both A→B and B→A requests are forced to acquire the same first row regardless of which way the transfer is going, the second transaction simply queues and waits behind the first instead of each grabbing a different row and forming a cycle, so the deadlock cannot occur.
Transfers between disjoint account pairs never contend on the same row, so imposing a deterministic lock order costs nothing in throughput — full parallelism is preserved for unrelated transfers.

The fix should be verified by firing many concurrent A→B and B→A transfers on the same account pair under load and confirming zero `deadlock detected` errors, correct final balances on both accounts, and an intact `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)` invariant across the ledger.

In a saga orchestrator, writing the `saga_step` audit row only after the HTTP call to the downstream service returns — on both the success and failure branches — means no row exists at all for the entire duration of that call.

The blind window sits between the moment the downstream service (wallet-service) applies its side effect (the debit) and the moment `sagaSteps.save(...)` actually executes; a crash inside that window leaves zero trace that the step was ever attempted.

Because there is no row until after the call resolves, a recovery scan cannot distinguish a step that never ran from one that ran and never got a chance to record its result — both look identical: absence of a row.

That ambiguity leaves the recovery process with no basis to decide whether to resume the step or run a compensating transaction, so a real debit can end up applied against the wallet with nothing in the durable log to account for it.

The correct ordering is write-ahead: persist a `saga_step` row with status `started` before the HTTP call to wallet-service is made, then update that same row to `ok` or `failed` once the response (or error) comes back.

Write-ahead ordering makes the durable `saga_step` table, rather than the in-memory stack frame of the `call()` function, the actual source of truth for what the orchestrator was doing when it crashed.
A `started` row with no subsequent `ok`/`failed` update is not leftover noise — it is precisely the marker a recovery scan looks for to identify an in-doubt step that needs follow-up.

Once an in-doubt `started` row is found, the orchestrator can query wallet-service using the `sagaId` plus step identifier as an idempotency key to determine whether the debit actually applied, and only then decide to resume the saga or trigger compensation.

Balances stored in minor units (cents, VND, satoshi) routinely exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1) once an account grows large enough, and JavaScript's `Number` type cannot represent integers beyond that boundary exactly.

Coercing a minor-unit string balance through `Number(...)` before subtracting, as in `Number(truthBalance) - Number(ledgerBalance)`, rounds to the nearest representable double once the value crosses that boundary, producing a computed drift that is off by whole units of currency with no error or warning.

The reconciliation endpoint returns `drift` as a JSON number rather than a string, so even a correctly computed backend value gets re-coerced into floating point a second time by any client that deserializes that field, doubling the exposure to precision loss.

The write path carries an identical defect: `parseAmount` calls `parseFloat(raw)` on a transfer amount, so a large transfer can be rounded before it ever reaches the ledger, corrupting the very entries the reconciliation job is meant to check.

This class of bug is more dangerous than a typical crash because it is completely silent — nothing throws, no assertion fails, and the system just writes a compensating entry with a slightly wrong amount, so the double-entry invariant can drift for weeks before anyone notices.

The fix is to perform every arithmetic step on money — parsing, subtraction, and any derived compensating amount — using `BigInt` instead of `Number`, and to parse with `BigInt(raw)` so that malformed input like `"12.5"` throws instead of being silently truncated.

Every money field must be serialized back out as a JSON string rather than a JSON number, since no numeric JSON representation can survive re-coercion by a downstream consumer without risking the same precision loss.

Correctness should be verified by seeding a drift value above 2^53, asserting that the computed drift and compensating amount are exact to the unit, and asserting that the response body carries those amounts as strings rather than numbers.
A module-level `const breakers = new Map()` lives only in the heap of the single Node.js process that created it, so its contents never cross a process boundary.

When a service runs as multiple horizontally-scaled worker replicas, each replica boots its own empty Map, meaning every replica ends up with an independent, disconnected view of circuit state for the same host.

Concretely, once replica B accumulates enough failures against a host and flips its local entry to `open`, replica A's own Map has no record of that — A keeps calling `allowRequest` and sending jobs to a host that is already known to be down.

A circuit breaker that only protects one process's private view of a host, rather than the host itself across the whole deployment, defeats the actual purpose of a circuit breaker in a multi-replica system.

Any deploy, crash, or scale-down destroys the process heap, so all breaker state — fail counts and `openUntil` timestamps included — is silently reset to `closed` on restart, with no signal that a previously-open circuit ever existed.

Circuit-breaker state (open/closed status, failure counts, cooldown expiry) is inherently shared, cross-replica state rather than per-worker local state, so it belongs in a store external to any single process.

The fix is to delete the in-memory Map and keep the same four pieces of state — state, fails (with a time window), a probe gate, and openUntil — as Redis keys per host (e.g. `circuit:state:<host>`, `circuit:fail:<host>`, `circuit:probe:<host>`, `circuit:openUntil:<host>`), read and written through a shared Redis client so every replica sees the same data.
A `SET circuit:probe:<host> 1 NX EX <ttl>` style key acts as a single-probe gate that stops more than one replica from sending a half-open recovery probe to the same host at the same time.

The fix is proven by running two worker instances against the same Redis, tripping the breaker via 3 failures through instance A's `recordFailure`, then calling `allowRequest` on instance B for that same host and asserting it also returns `false` — showing both instances now read one shared key instead of two independent Maps.

Plain `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` with no `SKIP LOCKED` takes row locks on the matched rows, and any other transaction whose identical query matches the same rows must wait for those locks to release rather than moving on to a different set of rows.

When two poller replicas issue the exact same `ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE` query, the second replica ends up blocked behind the first replica's lock on the same top-N rows, so the two replicas execute serially instead of in parallel — this is why combined throughput does not improve with a second replica.

Adding `SKIP LOCKED` to the claim query (`... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) makes a poller skip rows already locked by another transaction and claim the next available rows instead, so concurrent pollers partition the pending set into disjoint batches and genuinely run in parallel.

The `UPDATE status = 'in_flight'` must run inside the same transaction as the claiming `SELECT`, before `COMMIT`, so that a row is marked as taken the instant it is claimed — this is what stops a later poller from re-claiming the same row once locks release.

`SKIP LOCKED` is a concurrency mechanism that turns a SQL table into a scalable multi-consumer work-queue; it fixes throughput and prevents double-claiming under normal operation, but it is not by itself an exactly-once delivery guarantee.

Because `SKIP LOCKED` does not cover the crash-mid-delivery case, a row claimed and flipped to `in_flight` that never completes delivery needs a separate recovery mechanism — such as a watchdog that resets stuck `in_flight` rows after a timeout — together with the receiver's idempotency cache to guard against duplicate delivery.

Verifying the fix requires running multiple poller replicas concurrently against the same table under load and confirming that claimed-rows-per-second scales roughly linearly with the number of replicas, instead of flatlining the way it does with plain `FOR UPDATE`.

Correctness of the fix also requires confirming that no single row ID is ever claimed by two replicas at the same time, for example via an assertion or a uniqueness check across replicas' claimed batches.

Computing an HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and running a constant-time comparison happens before the timestamp window is checked, so every incoming request pays for that crypto work regardless of whether it will ultimately be rejected.

Under a flood of stale or replayed requests, all of them are guaranteed to fail the timestamp window check, yet the receiver still performs the full HMAC computation and constant-time comparison first - burning CPU on work whose outcome was already sealed by the clock.

The window check only needs the timestamp already present in the parsed signature header and the current clock - no secret and no cryptographic work - which makes it effectively free compared to recomputing an HMAC over the body.

Moving the window check (`age > WINDOW_SECONDS`) to run immediately after parsing the header, before calling `sign()` and `constantTimeHexEqual`, lets stale requests be rejected without paying any crypto cost, while requests that survive the check still go through full signature verification.

The reorder is a pure change in cost, not in behavior: a stale timestamp was always rejected and a forged-but-in-window signature is still caught by the constant-time compare, so nothing that used to be accepted becomes rejected or vice versa.

Keeping `constantTimeHexEqual` for requests that pass the window check preserves the timing-attack resistance of the signature verification - only the order of the two checks changes, not the comparison method itself.

The fix can be verified by flooding the endpoint with out-of-window requests before and after the reorder: CPU and latency scale with the flood before the change and stay roughly flat afterward, since rejection now happens on a cheap timestamp comparison instead of a full HMAC computation.
A follow-up test with genuinely valid, in-window, correctly-signed requests must still succeed after the reorder, confirming that legitimate traffic is unaffected by the change.

HMAC signatures are computed over raw bytes, not over JSON semantics — the algorithm has no concept of "the same data," so any re-serialization that changes whitespace, indentation, or key order produces a completely different signature even though the parsed object is logically identical.

On the sender side, `JSON.stringify(payload)` is used to compute the signature, but a later "reformat" step runs `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body), null, 2)` before the actual HTTP POST — this produces a second, differently-formatted string, so the bytes that get signed are not the bytes that actually go out over the wire.

On the receiver side, the framework's body parser (e.g. Nest's default JSON parser) has already parsed the incoming request into an object before the handler runs, discarding the original wire bytes; re-stringifying that parsed object with `JSON.stringify(req.body)` yields yet a third, independently-formatted byte sequence rather than what the client actually sent.

Because the sender signs one byte sequence, sends a second, and the receiver reconstructs and signs a third, the two computed HMACs can never match regardless of whether the shared secret is correct — the 401 "signature mismatch" is a serialization bug, not an authentication or secret-mismatch bug.
The correct fix on the sender is to remove the reformat step entirely and transmit the exact same string that was signed, so no re-serialization happens between signing and sending.

The correct fix on the receiver is to capture the raw, unmodified request body before any JSON parsing occurs (e.g. enabling `rawBody: true` when bootstrapping the Nest app and reading `req.rawBody`) and compute the HMAC over those literal bytes instead of re-stringifying the already-parsed `req.body`.

"Logically equal JSON" (same keys and values) and "byte-identical payload" (the exact same byte sequence) are distinct properties, and only byte-identical payloads produce matching HMAC signatures — any middleware, proxy, or serializer that parses and re-emits the body between the signing step and the verification step breaks this guarantee.

Fixing the bug should be verified end-to-end by re-sending a webhook request and confirming the receiver now returns 200 instead of 401, and further confirmed by diffing the exact bytes the sender signed against the exact raw bytes the receiver read to prove byte-for-byte identity rather than just visual similarity.

BullMQ treats every uncaught throw inside a job processor as a failed attempt and increments job.attemptsMade, unless the job was already rescheduled with job.moveToDelayed(...) before that throw — a plain throw new Error('circuit open') is indistinguishable from the receiver genuinely rejecting the call.

During a sustained downstream outage the circuit stays open (or keeps re-tripping from a failed half-open probe) across many consecutive delivery cycles for the same event, so each skipped cycle still burns one attempt — it takes several circuit-open cool-downs, not a single throw, to exhaust attemptsMade and park the event in dead_letter with attempts: 3 even though the receiver never actually saw the request.

The correct fix is a strict ordering rather than a different mechanism: await job.moveToDelayed(Date.now() + delay, token) must happen FIRST so BullMQ knows the job is already rescheduled, and only THEN should new DelayedError() be thrown — DelayedError is BullMQ's explicit 'already handled, don't count this' signal.

Thrown before moveToDelayed, or thrown as a plain Error at all, BullMQ has no way to distinguish the circuit-open skip from an ordinary failure and still counts it toward attemptsMade — the ordering, not the error type alone, is what makes the skip invisible to the retry accounting.

A circuit-open skip is an infrastructure decision made without ever contacting the receiver, while a failed attempt should only be recorded when the receiver was actually reached and rejected the request; conflating the two quietly corrupts the dead-letter table's meaning as a record of genuinely-exhausted deliveries.

The circuit's half-open state admits exactly one probe per cool-down, so if that probe request reuses the same soft-skip code path before its success or failure is recorded, it risks being miscounted as a burned attempt too — the fix needs to close that gap, not just the plain circuit-open branch.

With the ordering corrected, attemptsMade stays flat for as long as the circuit remains open no matter how many cool-down cycles the outage spans, and only events the receiver actually rejected MAX_ATTEMPTS times ever reach the dead-letter table.

A deterministic check for this fix drives a downstream outage across several consecutive circuit-open cool-downs and asserts the attempt counter stays unchanged throughout, then confirms that only events for which the receiver genuinely returned failures accumulate attempts and eventually land in dead_letter.
Opening a database transaction and then performing a network call before COMMIT stretches the transaction's lifetime to cover the entire HTTP round-trip to an external receiver.

While that transaction stays open, the connection checked out from the pool is unavailable to any other request, and the row locks taken by the preceding INSERTs on orders and outbox_event remain held for the same duration.
A slow or hanging receiver therefore degrades the whole application by starving the connection pool, even though the receiver's behavior has nothing to do with the database itself.

Coupling commit success to the HTTP call's outcome reintroduces the send-then-commit / commit-then-send dilemma the outbox pattern exists to remove: if the POST throws, the catch block rolls back both INSERTs, but the receiver may already have received and started acting on the request before that throw happened, or the process could crash after axios.post resolves but before COMMIT runs — leaving a webhook delivered for an order that will never exist in the database.

The correct shape is for publish() to perform only the two writes — insert the order row and an outbox_event row with status='pending' — then COMMIT and return, since the row's job at that point is to durably record intent to send, not to actually send.

Actual delivery belongs to a separate poller that claims pending rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside its own short transaction and performs the axios.post call outside any transaction boundary tied to the write path.

This separation decouples delivery latency from the write path: callers of publish() get a fast response the instant the two rows are durable, and a hung or slow receiver only ever stalls the poller's worker, never a connection borrowed for someone else's request.

The decoupling can be verified the same way the outbox's durability guarantee is normally checked: kill the process right after the outbox row commits but before the poller's next tick, restart it, and confirm the poller still claims and delivers that row.

Calling `subscribe` on every `chat:join` without first checking whether the room already has local members re-issues a Redis SUBSCRIBE for a channel this node is already listening on, which is redundant work with no corresponding benefit.

Tearing down only the Socket.IO room membership on disconnect while leaving the Redis subscription in place means the node keeps listening to a room's pub/sub channel long after its last local member has left.

Without a per-room reference count, a node has no way to distinguish 'already subscribed, one more local member joined' from 'not yet subscribed, first member joined' — so join can only ever re-subscribe blindly and leave can only ever forget to unsubscribe.

A stale subscription is not free: every message published to that room's channel still reaches the node, gets JSON-parsed, and is then discarded because there are zero local sockets to deliver it to, which is exactly the wasted work that sharded pub/sub was meant to avoid.
Because rooms continuously empty and refill in a chat system, a node's subscription set that never shrinks only grows over the node's lifetime, so the leak is unbounded rather than a one-time cost.

The correct invariant is that a node's Redis subscription set must exactly mirror the set of rooms it currently has local members in — subscribing to rooms with no local members wastes CPU and bandwidth, while failing to subscribe to rooms that do have local members causes missed message delivery.

The fix is a per-room reference count (e.g. a `Map<string, number>`) rather than a boolean or set-presence check: `subscribe` is called only on the 0 -> 1 transition when the first local member joins a room, and `unsubscribe` is called only on the 1 -> 0 transition when the last local member leaves; subsequent joins or partial leaves just adjust the counter without touching Redis.

The fix can be verified operationally with Redis introspection commands such as `PUBSUB CHANNELS` and `PUBSUB NUMSUB` run right after a room's last member leaves — the channel should disappear from the subscribed list and `NUMSUB` should drop to match only the nodes that still have a local member in that room.

When a gateway calls `io.to(room).emit(...)` once per incoming message, the cost lands on the gateway's own event loop, not on Redis: Socket.IO has to encode the payload and fan it out across every socket in the room on each call, so a 50-message burst for one room means 50 full encode-and-broadcast passes back to back.

A `RoomBatcher` fixes this by decoupling arrival from delivery: instead of emitting from the listener directly, an `enqueue(envelope)` step appends the message to a per-room buffer and arms a `setTimeout(windowMs)` — typically around 50ms — the moment that room's buffer goes from empty to non-empty, so later messages in the same window simply ride the already-armed timer.

When the timer fires, the buffer flushes exactly once as `io.to(room).emit("chat:batch", buffer)`, turning what would have been N separate encode+broadcast operations into a single call carrying however many messages accumulated in that window.
A `maxSize` cap on the buffer forces an early flush if a burst is larger than the window can hold, so the fix behaves safely under unbounded traffic instead of letting the buffer grow indefinitely.

The flush timer should be `unref()`'d so a pending flush never keeps the Node process alive at shutdown, and the batcher should still flush any remaining per-room buffers on `SIGTERM` rather than silently dropping messages that were waiting on a timer.

Batching trades a small amount of delivery latency — up to one `windowMs` — for a large reduction in operation count: the number of encode+broadcast calls drops from N to roughly `ceil(N / maxSize)`, while the total bytes transferred stay essentially the same since the same messages still go out, just grouped.

For chat specifically, a delay of tens of milliseconds is imperceptible to a human, which is what makes this trade-off acceptable even though it does introduce real, non-zero latency compared to immediate per-message delivery.

Correctness of the fix can be checked by flooding a room with many messages in quick succession and confirming both that the resulting batch count is far smaller than the message count (proving coalescing actually happened) and that every member of the room still receives every message with none dropped.

Redis sizes a bitmap string to the largest bit offset ever addressed by SETBIT, not to the number of bits actually set, so calling SETBIT with a raw 64-bit snowflake userId as the offset forces allocation up to that offset regardless of how many users are actually online.

A bitmap's one-bit-per-user economy only holds when the offset space is dense and bounded; snowflake ids are sparse and can reach into the quintillions, so using them directly as offsets turns a cheap presence structure into a near-empty, potentially exabyte-scale allocation.

The fix is to remap each userId to a small, contiguous index rather than changing the underlying presence model - a Redis-backed sequence (INCR on a counter key) or a HASH mapping userId to a compact index can be looked up or allocated on connect, and SETBIT/GETBIT then operate on that index instead of the raw id.

Remapping to a dense index preserves exact BITCOUNT semantics: the online count is still computed by counting set bits, and the one-bit-per-user presence model is unchanged - only the meaning of the offset shifts from "this exact userId" to "this user's assigned slot".

An alternative to maintaining a userId-to-index lookup table is sharding the bitmap by id range (for example dividing userId by a fixed bucket size) into separate keys like presence:online:<range>, which bounds each shard's maximum offset independently.
When sharding by id range, computing the total online count requires summing BITCOUNT across every shard touched by online users, rather than a single BITCOUNT call.

Correctness after the fix should be verified by checking that MEMORY USAGE (or DEBUG OBJECT) on the online-presence key scales with the number of connected users rather than with the magnitude of their raw ids, and that BITCOUNT still equals the true online headcount.
A userId-to-index mapping introduces its own lookup on every connect and disconnect, so where that mapping is stored and how it is kept consistent across nodes matters for avoiding a new bottleneck.

Redis presence tracking that stores a single online/offline bit per user only works correctly when each user has exactly one connection at a time; the moment a user has multiple simultaneous connections (phone and laptop, or two browser tabs), the single bit can no longer represent their true state.

A user's real online status is the union of every connection they currently have open, not a reflection of whichever connection most recently changed state — so a disconnect on one device should only affect the shared bit if it was that user's last remaining connection.

Calling `SETBIT presence:online <userId> 0` unconditionally inside `disconnect()` means the very FIRST disconnect for a user clears the bit, even while other connections for that same user are still alive on other nodes — the correct behavior is for only the LAST disconnect to clear it.

The missing piece is a per-user reference count: without tracking how many live connections a user currently has, `connect()` and `disconnect()` have no way to distinguish 'this was one of several connections' from 'this was the only connection.'

The fix is a per-user connection counter stored in Redis (e.g. `presence:conn:<userId>`), incremented with `INCR` on every `connect()` and decremented with `DECR` on every `disconnect()`, so the counter reflects the total number of live connections across the whole cluster.

The online bit should only be written on the edges of that counter: `SETBIT ... 1` fires solely on the 0-to-1 transition (the first connection appearing), and `SETBIT ... 0` (plus removing the counter key) fires solely on the 1-to-0 transition (the last connection disappearing) — connects and disconnects in between just adjust the count without touching the bit.

The counter must live in shared Redis rather than in either node's local process memory, because a user's connections can land on different nodes behind a load balancer; each node only sees its own in-memory state, so only a value that every node can atomically read and update turns 'does this user have any connection left anywhere in the cluster?' into one race-free, globally consistent answer.

Correctness of the fix can be verified by opening two connections for the same user on two different nodes and confirming the online count stays at 1, closing one connection and confirming the user still shows online, and only seeing the state flip to offline once the very last connection closes.

Redis INCR and SET NX are each individually atomic, but calling INCR before SET NX means every accept() call — including a retry of an already-seen messageId — claims a fresh sequence number before the system ever checks whether the message is a duplicate.

When accept() writes the message into the log (ZADD) right after INCR but before the dedup check runs, a retried message ends up stored twice in the log under two different seq values, even though both writes carry identical content.
SET NX on the dedup key is the only call that actually knows whether a given messageId has already been accepted; it therefore must run and be evaluated before any state-mutating step, not after.

Reordering the operations so SET NX runs first turns accept() into a real gate: a null return means the key already existed, so the handler can load and return the previously stored message immediately, without ever calling INCR or ZADD.
Only the caller for which SET NX succeeds (the first writer) should proceed to INCR and ZADD, which limits seq claiming and log writes to genuinely new messages.

Because SET NX and INCR each remain atomic on the same Redis instance, putting the dedup gate first is enough to guarantee that even concurrent retries of the same messageId consume exactly one seq and produce exactly one log row — the atomicity of the individual commands is not sufficient on its own when their order is wrong.

A regression test for this fix sends the same messageId twice (sequentially and concurrently) and asserts that the per-room seq counter advances exactly once and the log holds exactly one row for that message.

The root cause here is not a wrong choice of Redis command — both INCR and SET NX are correct primitives on their own — it is the sequencing of two correct operations, a distinct class of bug from picking the wrong API.

Calling `this.io.to(payload.room).emit(...)` immediately inside the `chat:send` handler already delivers the message to every socket joined to that room on the local node, before any pub/sub round-trip happens.

Because every node — including the node that received the original `chat:send` — subscribes to the same backplane channel, publishing the envelope causes the origin node's own subscription handler to fire and deliver the identical envelope a second time to sockets it already served directly.

The result is an asymmetric duplicate-delivery bug: clients on the origin node receive the message twice while clients on other nodes receive it only once, which is why it can pass a single-node smoke test and only surfaces once two clients share the same node.

The correct design keeps `chat:send` on a single path: the handler should only publish to the backplane, and delivery to any socket — local or remote — should happen exclusively inside the subscription's message callback, so same-node and cross-node clients share identical code.

Re-adding a direct `emit` call at send time reintroduces exactly the 'is the recipient local or remote?' special case the publish/subscribe backplane exists to remove, splitting one delivery route into two competing ones.

The fix is to delete the `this.io.to(payload.room).emit(...)` line from the handler entirely, keep only the `publish` call, and let the subscriber's callback perform all delivery — stamping fields like `originNode` and `deliveredBy` on the envelope there so the routing hop is provable rather than assumed.

Routing every delivery, even same-node, through the backplane costs one extra round-trip, which is an acceptable trade for eliminating a duplicate-delivery bug and the local/remote branching that caused it.

Correct behavior can be confirmed by connecting two clients to the same node and checking that each receives exactly one `chat:message` per send, then repeating with a client on a different node to confirm it also receives exactly one copy.

A queue configured with unbounded (or near-infinite) `attempts` and no `removeOnFail` handling has no mechanism to stop retrying a job that always fails — a malformed payload that makes the processor throw on every attempt just keeps looping instead of ever landing in a failed/dead-letter set.

When a worker's concurrency is effectively pinned to one job at a time, a single poison job stuck in an endless retry loop permanently occupies that worker slot, starving every legitimate job queued behind it — this is exactly the symptom of one worker pinned at "processing" the same job for hours at 100% CPU.

Accepting `@Body() body: any` in the controller and mapping `channels` directly into queued jobs with no DTO or `ValidationPipe` means invalid input — an unrecognized channel, an empty message — is never rejected at the boundary; it reaches Redis and becomes the root cause of the processor throwing repeatedly downstream.

Validating at the producer boundary — a DTO with `@IsEnum` on `channels` and `@IsNotEmpty()` on `message`, wrapped in `ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true })` — rejects a bad request with HTTP 400 before it is ever enqueued, which is a distinct and complementary fix from bounding retries on the worker side.

Replacing an unbounded `attempts` setting with a realistic finite number plus exponential backoff, and enabling `removeOnFail`, gives an exhausted job a defined stopping point: it lands in the failed set for inspection instead of cycling forever between retry and processing.

In a PR review, worker starvation from an unbounded retry loop and the missing dead-letter escape are blockers because they can cause an outage, while something like a hardcoded port or a magic-number limit is a nitpick that does not change runtime behavior under failure.

Treating an unbounded retry setting as an obvious bug rather than checking intent risks decreeing over a possibly deliberate choice — someone may have wanted infinite retries for genuinely transient failures — so asking whether the behavior was intentional is part of a thorough review.

The fix is verifiable concretely: a request with an invalid channel should return HTTP 400 and never reach `addBulk`/Redis, and a payload that always fails processing should exhaust its attempts and increase the failed-set count by exactly one instead of ever returning to the active or waiting state.

A `findOne` followed by a separate `insert` costs two network round-trips to the relational database for every single message, and since this dedup check runs on every send, it puts the database on the hot path for the system's highest-frequency operation.

`findOne` and `insert` are two independent commands rather than one atomic operation, so there is a check-then-act (TOCTOU) window between them: two workers can each run `findOne`, each see no existing row, and both proceed to `insert` and call `send`, producing a duplicate delivery even though the code appears to guard against it.

A unique constraint on `messageId` only converts the race into a database error on the second `insert` after the fact — it does not stop the second worker from having already called `send()` before that insert fails, so it detects the duplicate rather than preventing it.

The fix is to stop treating deduplication as a database read-then-write and instead perform it as a single atomic Redis command, `SET dedup:{messageId} 1 NX EX <ttl>`: because the existence-check and the write happen inside one atomic operation, there is no window in which two concurrent workers can both observe the key as absent.

The `NX` flag makes the `SET` succeed only if the key does not already exist, so the command itself returns success (`"OK"`) to exactly one caller when multiple workers race on the same `messageId`, and every other caller receives `null` and skips sending.

This is a single round-trip and an O(1) key lookup, compared to the original approach's two round-trips against an indexed table, which is what removes the database from the per-message hot path at peak throughput.

The `EX` option attaches a self-expiring TTL to the dedup key, so the dedup store does not grow without bound the way a permanent `sent_messages` table would, since old entries fall out of Redis automatically once the TTL elapses.

Correctness of the fix should be verified by firing the same `messageId` concurrently from multiple workers and asserting that exactly one of them acquires the key and sends, and by comparing round-trip count and latency under load against the original SELECT-then-INSERT path to confirm the throughput improvement.

Keying the rate-limit bucket strictly per user×channel (`rl:<recipient>:<channel>`) correctly isolates one recipient's limit from another's, but Redis Cluster maps that single literal key to exactly one hash slot on exactly one shard.

When one recipient goes viral or one channel gets hammered, every request for that pair funnels through the same key, so its EVAL calls saturate one shard while every other shard in the cluster sits idle — the bottleneck is single-key contention, not total Redis capacity.

The fix is to shard the hot key into N sub-buckets (`rl:<recipient>:<channel>:<shard>` for shard in 0..N-1), each sized to `bucketCapacity/N` and `refillAmount/N`, and route each incoming request to one sub-bucket (round-robin, or hashing a request-local id mod N).
Running the same Lua script against just the routed sub-bucket keeps the per-request check O(1) and local, with no cross-shard read needed to decide allow or deny.

Because the N sub-bucket keys naturally land on different hash slots, a viral recipient's load spreads across up to N shards instead of pinning one; when the total remaining is needed (an admin dashboard, a debug endpoint), it is computed by summing the token count across all N sub-buckets.

Splitting one shared bucket into N even slices is a real trade-off, not a free win: a burst that would have fit under the single bucket can now be rejected if it lands unevenly across sub-buckets, trading some burst-smoothing accuracy for horizontal spread across shards.

For genuinely extreme keys — traffic blowing past every sub-bucket instantly — a cheap in-memory approximate counter at the edge can reject obviously-over-limit requests before they ever issue a Redis EVAL, so Redis only sees traffic with a real chance of being allowed.
Moving the rate-limit Redis onto its own instance, separate from the queue Redis used for job dequeue, prevents a hot rate-limit shard from also starving unrelated queue traffic.

The sharding change should be validated with a load test that drives one hot key alone, measuring per-key p99 latency before and after sharding, and confirming the summed aggregate across the N sub-buckets still enforces the original limit.

When a producer packs every requested channel into the data of a single queue job, the broker only has one pass/fail outcome to react to — it cannot tell that push already succeeded and only email needs another try.

A for-loop that awaits push, then email, then sms inside one processor function has no isolation between channels: an exception thrown while sending email propagates out of the processor and is treated as a failure of the entire job, not just the email step.

Because the retry unit in a job queue is the job itself, retrying that failed job re-runs the processor from the top — so push, which already sent successfully, fires again and reaches the user as a duplicate notification.

The mismatch driving this bug is that the desired unit of retry is one channel, while the actual unit of retry the queue provides is one job; bundling multiple channels into a single job collapses that distinction.

The structural fix is fan-out at the producer: instead of enqueuing one job whose data holds an array of channels, enqueue one separate job per channel (for example via a bulk-add call), using the channel as the job name and giving each job only that channel's payload.
With one job per channel, a failure in the email job causes the broker to retry only that job; the push and sms jobs already completed independently and are left untouched, so they cannot be re-sent.

Wrapping each provider call in a try/catch that swallows the error is not a valid fix, because it prevents the failure from ever surfacing to the queue — the email job is never marked failed, so it is never retried, and the notification is silently lost instead of duplicated.

A meaningful way to verify the fix is to enqueue a multi-channel request where the email provider fails on its first attempt, then confirm push and sms were each delivered exactly once while only the email job shows a retry that eventually succeeds.

Keeping a rate limiter's remaining-token count on a private field of a service instance means every replica running behind a load balancer holds its own independent copy of that count, so the aggregate throughput allowed across all replicas is roughly N times the intended per-key limit.

In-memory counter state does not survive a process restart: a redeploy or crash-restart re-initializes the field to its starting capacity, silently resetting the limiter to full even though no time-based refill was actually earned.

Implementing a Redis-backed limiter as a plain `GET` followed by a plain `SET` is not atomic — the two calls are separate network round trips, so two concurrent requests can both read the same stored token count, both compute the same decremented value, and both write it back, losing one decrement and letting more requests through than the limit allows (a TOCTOU race).

The fix is to collapse the entire read-refill-decrement-write sequence into a single Lua script executed via Redis `EVAL`, because Redis runs each Lua script to completion on its single command thread, so no other client's command can interleave in the middle of the sequence.

The bucket must be keyed per logical entity being limited (for example `user:channel`) so that every replica reads and writes the same shared counter in Redis instead of each maintaining its own state, and the key should carry a TTL/expiry so an idle bucket is cleaned up automatically instead of accumulating in Redis forever.

Overshooting a provider's send-rate limit is a production-severity blocker rather than a style nitpick, because the sending IP or account can get throttled or blocked by the notification provider/carrier, taking down message delivery for the whole system.

This class of bug passes cleanly in a single-instance local or test environment because there is only one process and no real concurrent network round trip to expose the race — it only manifests once the service is actually scaled out to multiple replicas under concurrent load.

Verifying the fix requires a concurrency test: fire capacity-plus-one requests at the same key simultaneously (ideally from at least two separate instances or connections) and assert that exactly one request is rejected, which proves the counting is atomic and shared rather than racy or per-process.

A catch block that simply rethrows an error so the queue's built-in attempts and exponential backoff retry the job is not the same as failover: it re-invokes the exact same primary provider after each backoff delay, so if the primary is genuinely down, every retry hits the same dead endpoint again and the recipient waits through several seconds of dead time for nothing.

Genuine failover switches to a fallback provider within the same attempt — catching the primary's failure and immediately calling the fallback before the job handler returns — rather than letting the error escape to the queue and waiting on a scheduled retry; only when both the primary and the fallback fail should the error propagate to the broker for an actual job-level retry.
